That we shall return to our pretty graceful flowing robes again, goes without say- ing, and in purchasing lengths of material, we should bear this fact in mind, and also possess ourselves of an extra yard or two, in view of possible renovations. A Use for Oriental Shawlv.—The woman nho , possesses an Oriental shawl,the more ancient the better ! —provided of course it is in a good state of preserva- tion—need look no further for an up-to-date evening wrap. Skilful modistes are looping these shawls here and catching them there, until the effect is all the artistic conld desire. Moreover scissors being ignored entirely, and stitches carefully put in, no damage is • done to the shawls. The heavy handsome fringes are of course a splendid finish to these evening wr ,ps, and , add considerably to the richness of their appearance. Hat Strings.—Many milliners are introducing strings of tulle, chiffon, not, or black velvet to their creations, and no doubt to the young and pretty face they form a charming addition. By the woman too well past her I youth, and whose throat is no longer full and rounaed, strings can be worn to advantage, but all "in-betweens" they age. The yonng strings are for the most part , left quite loose, the elderly woman, on the contrary ties hers beneath her chin, and arranges a full bow at j the left side.

' The Queen's Excellent Health.—Queen Alexandra's share in public life is necessarily less coespicuous than was Queen Victoria's, but her Majesty never fails to accompany the Ring TA hen she thinks bef presence will give pleasure to the people, as on the occasion of the Stnte visits to Leeds and Bristol. Apart from the long journeys and protracted ceremonious functions, the Queen works RS hard and goes about as much as mcst women and yet happily we seldom it ever hear of her Majesty succumbing to any of the all too fashionable ailments of the day. Since the Queen came among us, she has known only one severe illness, and that in the early days of her married life. Unfortunately her Majesty has not bequeathed her robust health to her daughters, who have never been really strong, and the Princess Royal is again taking a sea voyage owing to bee dtlicate constitution. The Princesses Alexandra end Maud of Fife.—lt has been decided that the elder daughter of the Duke and Duchess of Fife is to join the Royal Circle at the early courts next year, after which a great deal of entertain- ing will be done in her honour. The Duchess of Fife is not likely to he able to he much with her daughters in their festive times to come, but Queen Alexandra will possibly take her granddaughters under her personal care, and then there is the Princess of Wales, and again, many other exalted relatives, all ready to give these bright winsome girls a happy time. Princess Alexandra who is in her eighteenth year, is deveted to sports of all kinds' and yachting in particular. She is tall and graceful and possesses charming manners, though, like her mother the Princess Royal, she is somewhat quiet and reserved when with strangers. Royalty in the Provinces.—The King and Queen, and the Prince and Princess of Wales, also have a number of provincial engagements on hand. Next week their majesties are to pay State visits to Leeds and Bristol, arriving at the latter city on Thursday. when the Ring will formally open the new docks at Avonmouth. Their Majesties will also take the opportunity to pay one or two private visits whilst in the west. The Examiner Saturday, July 4, 1908.
WOMAN'S REALM.
DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
THE NEW LADY DERBY.

The new Lady Derby, who has been Woman. of - the- Bedchamber to Queen 'Alexandra ever since the Accession, is, a notable addition to the number of Peeresses who may be counted as political hostesses, says the Skach. She was nurtured in an atmosphere of high politics, for be is the daughter of Louise, Dachess of Devon.. shire by', her first husband, the late Duke of Manchesfer, and thus she is the sister of Lady Gasford, Mary, Duehcss of Hamilton, and that most agreeable bachelor, Lord Clarks Montagu. She has two sons of fourteen a'nd twelve, at.d a daughter of sixteen.
FLOWERED Mustrx Pgtocx.

A garden-party frock of flowered muslin in dainty mauve colouring is the subject of our sketch. It is so simple in design that it would not present any great difficulty to the home dressmaker. The fulness of the skirt is arranged in tiny tucks set quite closely together; and at (ho hem there are two wide tacks. The full

rae bodice is /tiniest hidden by the crossover fichu, which is edged with a very narrow gull- IMg of its own material. It is draped across the figure to the left side, where it is passed be- neath the belt, and finishes in a long stole cad. At the back the other end is carried over .to the right side and treated in the same way. The belt is of soft mauve , satin. the buckles being covered with the same material.

div.head: HONOURS FOR WOMEN STUDENTS.
div.p: HONOURS FOR WOMEN STUDENTS.

High honours have been taken at Cambridge by women students this year. Miss Margery Long. of Girton College, who received much of her education at the North London Collegiate. School, obtained a place equal to fourth wrangler—a position only eclipsed by Miss Faw- cett many years ago when„as a Newnharn stu- dent site was listed above the senior wrangler, her success causing the greatest excitement throughout the country. Miss J. F. Cameron, a D.A. of Edinburgh and a Newnharn student, was placed equal to tenth wrangler, and a Gir- ton student, Miss L. W. Jones. to twentieth wrangler. In the Classical Tripes and ir. Part IL of the Natural Science Tripes several Girton and Newnham students have been placed in Class I. as a!so in the Mathematical Tripos, Part 1., under the new regulations. Two women hays also secured entrance scholarships at Uni- versity College, one f,or language and history being awarded to Miss L. W. Stone, of the High School, Stroud Green, and the Campbell Clarke Scholarship -fo; £4O for three years to Miss E. O'Rourke, of the City of London School.

It is little comfort to a modern woman, says the Lady's Pictorial, to be told that her "hour" is the evening, and that she "looks her beet" tho soft glow of artificial lamps and the distinc- tion of an evening gown. Now that our round of entertainments may commence with an early breakfast party, and not cease till we have lunched, motored, tea'd, dined, thcatred, and supped, in the interval between other engage- ments, woman has to go round the, clock: and something over, always conscious that she is ex- pected to look her best. DAINTY. BATHING COLIE.

As the holiday season approaches it is time to consider the subject of a pretty and suitable bathing costume, so this week we arc giving a suggestion, which is depicted in our sketch, carried out in shell-pink aiid white striped gala. tea. The knickers, which are almost hidden by tho extra long tunic, are attached to the short. waisted corsage. The edeeves aro planned in one with the bodice, and are bordered with bands

of plain pink linen and trimmed with linen. covered buttons. The rounded yoke is of the material cut on the cross, and is bordered at both edges with the bands of plain material. The bands are carried down the front of the bodice, and also down the front of the tunic, which is attached to the deep belt, cut on the cross and strapped with the plain coloured linen. The buttons and loops of cord on the bodica are merely used 28 decoration, as the costume fas- tens on the left shoulder, the shirt fastening- down the centre-front. WOMAN THE THINKER. • The Right Rev. the I.ord Bishop of Adelaide, preathing, at Southwark Cathedral from the text "Think on these things," said that a feature of the Pan-Anglican *Congress that had impressed

him was the attendance of women at those sec- tions of the congress which dealt with the Church and thought as compared with the at- tendance at those dealing with practical matters. At the latter men were in the majority, but at the former woLien predominated to the extent of ten women to on man./ Ile had observed the Famo tendency in hi s own diocese of Adelaide. It was women who cave time to thought; men in their various activities had no time to think, and to this wits due the lack of grafeth in the spiritual life which was a eharacteriAic of the age, while growth in other directions was so re- markable.

div.head: NOTEWORTHY TALRING MACHINE
div.p: NOTEWORTHY TALRING MACHINE
IMPROVEMENTS.

A new type of cylinder talking machine, rezently announced bi the Columbia Phonograph Company, Is certain very .soon to make the ordinary phonograph quite out of date, since it incorporates, for the first time in cylinder instruments, the special advantages of the disci 'style of talking machine which have hitherto led ibany purchasers to prefer the disc to the cylinder variety. Them advantages consist in an aluminium tone-arm and a large swinging, flower-horn. The tone- arm, by reason of its special form and the unique properties of aluminium as a sound transmitter, produces a tong very much fuller and richer thah the ordinary cOioder reproduction ; while the swinging horn may be turned at will in any direction instead of being held in one posi- tion by an awkward arrangement of crane and rubber tubing. The first model with the new equip- ment (the "Crown " Oraphophone) was., put out a month or two ago, and so popular did it immediately become, that a second tone-arm model (the" Coronet") has quickly followed. The "Coronet " has also on extra long mandrel to take all sizes of cylinder records including the 6in. " Premier" Columbia Records. A good idea of the compact appearanCe of these new tone-arm ,Orapbophones may be gained from the manu- facturers' advertisement which appears in this issue, while a postcard addressed "Columbia Phonograph Company. 64 and CG, Oxford-street, London, W.;" will bring an ill ustratgd leaflet giving full particulars.

DEATH OF "ALL BLACIZS' " SECRETARY. News was received on Monday by Mr. Mercer, secretary of the St. Helens Rugby Club, from one of the members of the " All Blacks'" team, that Mr. A. H. Baskerville, secretary of the New Zealand team, which toured hero last season, died in Sydney Hospital.

A bouquet of polo pink carnations was presented to the Lady Mayoress by bliss Amy Ifolme on behalf of the students. .... ._

1 I The PRINCIPAL said they had during the past year . entered into possession of their new wing—that part of i the building which was formerly inhabited by the !Clergy Daughters' School, who had now found fresh fields and pastures new. It had proved a great advan- tage to have that wing at their disposal as it had lenabled them to house more of their students under one roof. It had done away with the difEculty of having some of their students at a considerable distance from the College, and it had enabled them, by giving them more room, to make sundry improvements in the 11 College for the comfort and well-being of those who lived there. By calling the addition the Wilson-Patten Iwing they were commemorating a name which tronght : to their, recollection a great deal of generous help t i and kind friendship which had been shown by the j I family not only to that college but to many other 1; causes in this part of England. The opening 6! the 1 wing had set free from the uses of the college one of ; their hostels—Orford Hall—which had now entered ; upon a new phase of existence. They had been able !to place there those who were called certificated students—that was to say, teachers who had gained their certificate but wished to have a year's training in . a college. It was found extremely difficult in the past to fit in certificated students for the simple reason that the training college students had a course of two years and the certificated students a course of one year. The consequence wits that not many colleges cared to open their doers to eertificated students and now they at , Warrington were able to open et house on purpose or I them, they could have their own course and their own ee Balms. Warrington was the only place in Rngland ' \the:a that was done and be ventured to think it was an interesting experiment and he hoped it would prose successful. At all events it co-ordiunted the system of the college .and they felt that the Church of England had now provided for all classes of teachers who required the help of training in different directions. (Applause.) Alluding to the work of the year, Capon Stevenson quoted the opinion of the Archbishops inspector: I have never known the colleee doing better than it is now." The Government ispector said: "There is no doubt that the college un er your guidance, is doing as geed and valuable work as ever it did aed that the commendations which it has earned from, I may say, generations of training college inspectors continue to be fully deserved." The inspector of physical exercises said: " I think I am right in stating that the assessment of the students this year is above that of the two previous years. The , percentage of those assessed as excellent' or ' very good ' this year is far in excess of that obtained by me at any other college, either v here I personally give instruction or act as an examiner only." Continu- ing, Canon Stevenson said that last year he spoke of the now regulations, which had been brought out by the Government, sad which they felt created certain difficulties in their colleges. All through the year negotiations bad been going on very quietly and steadily with the Govern- ment and while they were not yet absolutely complete, lie thought he might say there was every reason-to hope that the Government was going to take a more conciliatory attitude and that a concordat would be arrived at by which they would be able to retain that which valued very highly indeed—the right to go On with their own religious teaching and worship after the manner and principles of their dear old Church. (Applause.) They did not with to look at the matter in a barrow spirit at all. It meant that they would have to make provision—and cheerfully make it—for those who were not members of the Church of England but it also meant, he took it, that they would be allowed to retain full liberty of teaching and worship for those who were members of the Church. (Applause.) The LORD MAYoR of Liverpool said be had a kind of feeling that a mere Lord Mayor had rio right to come and talk before a learned institution like that, but ho might plead as an excuse that the major part of his life had been spent in teaching, so that he really wished to spoils to the students as an old teacher and as one who loved teaching very much indeed. One often woudered, which was the most important profession in the world' —which profession bad tho most to do with human welfare and progress. Putting aside altogether the clerical profession—he did not wish to compare that With the others—he thought the profession which was at the present time and which still more in the future was going to be the most important of all prot fessions was that of the teacher. They were the people who were going ta build up the characters, the minds and habits cf the great mass of the people of i this country. That was a tremendous responsibility and a very honourable duty. They would have a large share in forming the religious beliefs for thousands end thousands of these who were to come after us. They would have a great share in teaching them morals and also all the arts of life. Very much of their success and prosperity during life and of their influence upon , the progress of the country would depend upon the 1 teaching they received in the schools. Be hoped the students were taking up teaching not merely as a means of livelihood, but also as a great national duty. In his 1 opinion the most important side of education was the religious side. If they could only impress the children ' not only by teaching but by example, with the great truth that religion was at the basis of everything in life and that morals, kindliness, love and gentleness were the essential basis of everything that was good, they would be doing a most valuable missionary work in the world. He hoped also that among their various lines of teaching they would be prepared to guide their pupils in regard to the simple facts of human life, in regard to sanitation and the principles which they must observe if they wanted to live healthily and wisely. He hoped they had all been taught, for example, some of those simple principles concerning diet. In our country there were certain huge delusions which were prevalent amongst the working people pat ticularly. The belief that alcohol was a necessary and useful part of diet was one of the great errors which it should be the teachers' dnty all their lives to trample down and dissi- pate as far as poscible. If they could only get the mass of the people to understand that there was no worse way of spending their money than on alcohol, they would have done a great deal. He was not speaking as a total abstainer, because be was not one, but he had a strong feeling from what he had Fern of the working people that the enormous sum of money that we spent ennually in intoxicant!, and which was mainly spent by the working people, was a grest national disaster, that it bought poverty, rni.sery and disease, and that with the money we spent upon it so much comfort, happiness end peace might be obtained. It was there- fore ruost important that they should teach every child in the schools that one great principle. The incuication of the value of fresh air, cleanliness, the need of exer- cise and a great many other points were also a necessary part of education. If they could once get those great facts thoroughly nuilerstood by the population they would see an astonishing change and a wonderful lessen- ing of the evils which existed at present. (Applause.) PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE. Prior to the Parish Council meeting the Parochial Committee met under the chairmanship of Mr. George Piliiug.—The Clerk said at the last meeting it was reported that the WarringtorrCorporation were issuing notices against putting liquor or any wet material into ash bins, and he was instructed to get out a draft notice to see if it met with the committee's approval for issue in this district. He found, however, that the com- mittee's by-laws would not per.nit them to issue en :h a notice, as there was DO by-law against placing liquor or wet materials in the ash bins.—On the proposition of Mr. Westbrook, seconded by Mr. Hallows, the Clerk was instructed to frame A by-law on the lines of the War- rington one,so that the Committee could put in it force. —A letter was read from the Northern Quarries Co., Bleckpool,stating that owing to a fire at their Silver- dale works some months ago they now found them- selves in considerable difficulty to complete a contract for the building of a school at St. Annes. As the school had to be completed in July they asked the Committee to kindly, allow them to suspend operations in connection with the paving work at Stockton Heath for a period of 10 days. They promised to return to the work with an increased staff, so that the contract would not be extended beyond the time the present staff would lake to complete it.—The Clerk said that Mr. Garnett, of Messrs. Wright, Garnett and Wright, surveyors for the work, replied that the contract waS already a month beyond the specified time, and under the circumstances they did not see how they could possibly help them by allowing them to withdraw the men.—The committee, however, decided to grant the company's request, and to ask them to proceed with the I work as quickly as pscsible.

div.head: SERVING A DRUNKEN MAN.
div.p: SERVING A DRUNKEN MAN.
Magistrates Think it a Technical
Offence.
WARRINGTON LICENSEE PAYS COSTS.

At the Borough Police Court, on Monday, before the 111-nyor (Alderman Smethurst), Mr. S. Wright, Mr. C. J. Holmes, Mr. G. Pilling, Mr. Wra. Roberts, Alderman Tinnion, Councillor Wilkinson, Councillor J. Evans, and Mr. W. Furness, Mary Ann Chrimes, Roebuck Hotel, Bridge-street, was summoned for serving a drunken person with beer.—Mr. Browne, solicitor, represented the defendant and pleaded not guilty. Detective Woollacott stated that at 105 p.m. on Monday, June 156, he was walking down Bridge-street when he saw a man named Thomas T3-man staggering about the pavement. Witness was forty yards behind, and he lost sight of the man. After looking about witness went into the Roebuck Hotel for the purpose of warning the landlady not to serve him. He then saw the man standing at the bar with a pint of beer in his hand. Witness called Mrs. Chrimes's attention to him, and .she said she served him with a pint of beer. Witness asked her if she noticed his condition, and she replied : "I thought I he was all right. The man is not drunk. He has been here some time." Witness said to Tyman : "Is this your beer ?" and he replied : " Yes, that's my pint of beer. I have paid for it and lam going to drink it." Witness took Tyman to the Police Station, and the following morning he was fined for being drunk. Later on tl:e Monday night witness saw Mrs.Chrimes and told her he had locked the man up for being drunk on licensed premises. She then said that Tyman came in and took another man's pint of beer. He had previ- ously been in the house that night and had a pint of beer. On Tuesday witness, in company with Sergeant I Heap. told Mrs. Chrimes she would be reported for permitting drunkenness and serving a drunken man. She replied, ' The man was not drunk. I did not serve him, the girl served him. He asked for a pint of beer, for which he paid 6cl.,and handed the beer to his friend. He left the house and returned shortly afterwards, picked up the beer for which he had paid for his friend, and commenced to drink it, when the officer came in." Mr. Browne said that was exactly correct. Mr. Browne : What right have you to take Mrs. Chrimes's jug out of her house? Witness : It is evidence of serving him (Tyman) with a pint of beer. Mr. Browne : Can you give me any justification ? Witness: The justification is that she Lad served
Mr. Browne : That is " stealing," in common language..
_ The Cbief Constable : She has her remedy for that, Sir.
Mr. Browne (to the detective) : You kept it, and you had no right to keep it or to take it. I never heard of such a thing. Witness said Mrs. chrimes could have it back after the case was over.

Mr. Browne said when Tyman appeared at the Police Court Dr. Fox said it as possible for a man to he drunk in his legs and not in his bead. Therefore, standing at the bar, Mrs. Chtimes might be 'unable to detect a man under the influence of drink. Witness : He (Tyman) was drunk all over. (Laughter). Sergeant Heel) gave evidence as to the visit on the Tuesday. Mrs. Chrimes said her instructions to her assistants were never to serve anybody who had the slightest suspicion of being drunk. ,On the night in question Tyman said: "Mrs. Chrirnes, give me a pint of beer for my mate. " Witness saw four or five men there, and they were perfectly sober. There was nothing to indicate that Tyman bad had too much drink. Ho took the beer and put it at the side of his mate and walked out without his change. Soon afterwards he came in again and commenced to drink his friend's beer' which he placed in front of him. lie then ruled for his change. She did not see Tyman stagger. She did not know Woollacott was a police officer a hen he came into the house.
in nns-w-er to Mr. W. Roberts, the Clerk said Tyruan, rchen before the mcgistrates, admitted that be uns drunk.

_ Miss Allen, barmaid, said le served Tyruan with a pint of Leer at p.m. At that time Mrs. Chrimcs was in her private room. When Mrs. Chritues served the Iran witness was in the kitchen, but she thought Mrs. Chrimes was quite justified in serving him. Mrs. Chrimes was very strict in serving people. Mr. Browne contended that Mrs. Chrimes took all reasonable precautions and was justified in serving Tyman. Mrs. Chrimes was a well-known Warringtonian, desirous of retiring with a clean record—and for a paltry !Id. she would not endanger her licence and her repute-

div.head: ,HINTS FOR THE HOfdE.
div.p: ,HINTS FOR THE HOfdE.

ISWEETBREAD CUTLETS. When the sweetbreads have heel properly prepared and simmered gently, drain them well, and when quite cold and firm cut them into small neat slices about one-third of an inch thick, and trim these as evenly as possible is shape and size; season them pleasantly with salt, pepper, very finely-minced onion, salad oil, and lemon-juice, and let them remain in a cool place for • about an hour, so as to imbibe the full flavour of the various ingredients; then egg and breaderionb them in the usual way, and fry in hot clarified fat until , coloured a lovely golden brown. When done enough, drain the cutlets thoroughly, arrange them neatly on a bOrder of daintily-prepared potato puree, 11l in the centre with green pens, French beans cut in lozenge shapes, buttered spinach, creamed cabbage, or any other nice green vegetable, pour richly-coloured tomato sauce Found about, and serve the whole very hot.. A RAGOUT, or SIVEETBREADS.—Prepare and cook the sweitbreads, and when quite cold cut them up into quarter of an inela dice; put these into a stew- pan with a liberal supply of prime streaky bacon pre- , viouely cooked and cut inte julienne shreds, two or three hard-boiled eggs, and yolks cut in quarters and the whites into shreds like the bacon, a teaspoonful of finely-minced boiled onion; a seasoning to taste of salt, pepper, and grated nutmeg, sufficient thick acreanly sauce—either maitre d'hael, parsley, tomato, or espagnol—to just nicely moisten the whole; then stir gently over a moderate fire until quite bubbling hot, after which dish up the ragout in the centre of a lightly browned potato border, arrange round about sonic mushrooms, which have been pleasantly seasoned and stewed gently in a little fresh pure butter until quite soft, and serve very hot. SwEnvenzan FRITTERS.—Ir sweetbreads are cooked specially for this dish, prepare the fritters, then, when they have lain in the eensonines sufficiently long, dip each one separately into thick rich frying batter, drop gently into boilint, clarified fat, and fry until just daintily browned, after which drain thoroughly, pile up on a very hotelish, garnish round about with curled bacon, slices of fresh lemon, and sprigs of parsley, and serve immediately, as fritters of any;kind should never be kept waiting. If, how- ever, it is more convenient, the fritters may be made as follows, and will be found equally, if not even more, dainty. Take the remains of cold cooked sweetbreads, no matter how small the pieces, andsup- pos,ng there are Coz., pat then' into a chopping bowl with •loz, of boiled ham or bacon and 2oz. of peeled mushrooms, and chop together very finely; then season nicely with salt, pepper, chopped parsley, and lemon-juice, and stir the mines into i,pt.. of thick, rich, frying batter; when thoroughly mixed drop the pre- paration about a tablespoonful at a time, into boil- ing clarified fat—sufficient ip quantity to entirely cover them—and fry lantil well swollen out and coloured a rich golden brown, when they must be carefully removed from the pan and thoroughly drained. Serve as quickly as possible, piled up high on a hot dish, garnished with slices of fresh lemon and sprigs of parsley. Daintily fried, hot, crisp croetons form an exceedingly nice accompaniment to sweetbread fritters of either kind; they should be neatly arranged on a hot dish-paper, and garnished with sprigs of parsley.—Marie, in the Ayrioltural Ga:rite.

_ CHILDREN'S RASHES.—These generally result from improper feeding, and a change of diet to more diges- tible food will often effect a care. At the same time, if a rash suddenly appears in a child not sub- ject to them, isolate it from the other children, and keep it very carefully from exposure to damp and cold till you find it is nothing serious or infectious. Nettle rash often looks like something much more serious. Eczema of some sort or another is the commonest skin trouble with children. The child usually needs cod-liver oil, malt ex'ract, or some specially nutritious diet or tonic. If it is bad, and forms a crust, especially in the hair, zinc ointment or vaseline are the bast outward applications. Be sure the child does not scratch. This only causes irritation and the spread of the mischief. Sulphur in some simple form is a good internal remedy. APPLE PUDDING A LA REINE,—Put a layer of pired, cored, and sliced apples about two inches. deep at the bottom of a deep dish, with sufficient sugar to sweeten ; somelemon mice and grated lemon peel, and a few cloves. Prepare a batter of half a pound of flour, a pint of milk, a thoroughly beaten egg, a pinch of salt, and a little baking powder. Pour this slowly and evenly over the apples. and bake in a quick oren for an hour. Sprinkle with sifted sugar, and serve hot. Cost, about 6d., enough for eight or nine people. A Dzuclocs WAY or PREPAELiG CIIOCOLATE.---• Take four,ounces of vanilla chocolate, one quart"of milk, three tablespoonfuls of hot water and one of sugar. Serape the chocolate finely. Boil your milk, and when at boiling point'stand it at one side for a few minutes while you carefullx mix the chocolate, sugar, and water in a china cup to a perfectly smooth paste. Put the milk on again, and stir in the paste. Bring, it to the boil, and then beat well with a whisk. Serve quickly, putting a little whipped cream into each cup, and filling up witht lie chocolate. If yon cannot get vanilla chocolae, yoa can use the plain, unsweetened, with a teaspoonful of vanilla extract, an more sugar. This is a Viennese method of pre- paring chocolate. Cost, about 6d. or id. SCALLOPED COCELES.—An excellent substitute for oysters. Wash in several waters, and leave in a basin of salt and water over night, covered; drain well, and put in a saucepan half full of boiling water; cook till the shells open, then remove at ence. Butter dish, strew with a layer of breadcriunbs, add a layer of cockles, with a little fish sauce and season- ing. Repeat layers, ending with one of crumbs. Put a few bits of butter here and there, and brown in the oven. Cost, 4d. or sd. for about six people. CARANIEL CCSTARD.—BoiI Goz. of brown sugar and one gill of Ivater together until it is dark brown. Warm a mould, butter it, and coat it over with the caramel by pouring in syrup and turninz, it round and round till the caramel Sets. Add lf pint of tin- skimmed milk, the yolks and whites of five eggs well beaten and mixed with the milk, and sugar to taste (all strained), pour into the mould, cover, and steam gently for one hour, not letting the water bubble. When quite cold turn out carefully. Average cost, Enough for five or six people. Mien-Mewl LEIIONADE.—.A. good home - made lemonade is made in the following way: Grate the peel of six lemons, pour a quart of boiling water on it ; let it stand some time, then add the juice of the lemons (take care not to let the lemon pips fall into the liquid). Sweeten it with clarified sugar, and ran it through a jelly bag. This will keep for two or three months. • '

div.head: Emmanuel Church—Sunday School Anniversary.
div.p: Emmanuel Church—Sunday School Anniversary.

Special services were held in the above church on Sunday last on the occasion of the Sunday School Anniversary. A choir of Sunday scholars took part in each service and sanganniversary hymns. The afternoon service was of a musical character, chiefly by the chil- dren. A large congregation gathered at this service. The Rev. F. Vaughan catechised the children on the distinctive features of the Reformed Episcopal Church, the children answering very clearly and distinctly, and I in each case giving Scripture proofs for their answers. The members of the Sunday School showed a good knowledge of tho Scriptures and the principles of the Chnrch.ln the evening the church choir gave the anthem " Sun of my Soul" (Turner) with taste and feeling. Very marked progress has teen made since the appoint- ment of 'Mr. J. W. Jowett as organist and choilmaster, whose work at the organ and with the choir is very much appreciated. The preacher for the day was the Rev. C. E. Wincott, of St. Philip's, Adlington. Mr. Wincott is a preacher of experience and ability and his earnest words were listened to by large and appre- ciative congregations. There was particular interest in this visit of Mr. Wincott, from the fact that his church and himself have just recently become atsliated with the Reformed Episcopal Church. His congrega- tion is a large and important one, and a great acquisi- tion to tbe ranks of Reformed churchmen. In spite of the intense heat the congregations were large and this vill be remembered as one of the most successful anniversaries ih the history of the church.

div.head: GREAT EXCURSION.
div.p: A GREAT EXCURSION.

The annual outing of the Beeston Humber Works is now becoming a Midland institution, and two heavily- laden trains drew out of Beeston station at 4 o'cl,mk the other morning loaded with happy holiday makers. Breakfast WAS served on the train ea route to Yarmouth where headquarters had been secured at the Queen's Hotel opposite the Brilliants Pier. At five o'clock the staff dinner was held at the Norfolk Artillery mess- house, and just befote midnight the return trains started for Beeston, taking tired but atilt happy holiday makers home. Not the least successful item in concoc- tion with the day was that it a.l.nohronised with the conclusion of the great 2,000 miles reliability trial in which the two Beeston Humber cars entered have scored such a magnificent success, being the only two cars entered by one maker to accomplish the complete trial without a single mechanical stop. The Beeston Humbers have made non-stop runs through every reliability trial of importance during the last three years and Saturday's brilliant triumph has made u fitting crown of glory for "the Best British Cars."

A Plucky Rescue. Some youths who cannot swim were silly enough on Wednesday to bathe in the Ship Canal near Latchford (where the water is about 26 ft. (!eep), when one of them suddenly disappeared. An alarm was raised, and with great promptness a married man named Alec Lord plunged into the mulky water without divesting himself of any clothing and fortunately made a gallant rescue. Such acts as these show what a Britisher is made of, also bow necessary it is for everyone to learn how to swim.

THE EXAMINER.
JULY 4th. 1878.

Daring the last few days LIBERALS AND there has been an inter- THE MINISTRY. mittent fire of corres- pondence between -Sir 4 i HENRY NORMAN, Mr. W. P. BYLE4, and other members of Parliament on the subject of the condi- tions under which some Liberal members occasion- ally indulge in the luxury of voting against the Government. Sir HENRY NonaraN complains, in effect, that the members in question taka an advantage of faithful Ministerialists like himself. He would like a little freedom on his own account, if it were obtainable without risk to the adminis- tration. It would, he Lints, be pleasant to him if, without placing the Government in any danger, ho could gratify those among his constituents who wish to make the Government go further than it -- feels justified in . going. But those, he rather ' more than hints, who do permit themselves to kick over the trae.-.‘s, do so at the expense of , their faithful colleagues, who have to support the Government all the more strenuously because certain of its nominal supporters wander MI into ways of their o wn .. Mr. BYLES'S argument in reply is the only on worth consideration. The Member for Salford sayg that he votes as he thinks right. He diVISIILIS any feeling of moral superiority over Sir LIENO NORMAN, As a rule he votes with the Govern- ment. He declares, indeed, that he votes with the Government much more frequently than his accuser • Obviously, however, that is an avoidance of the point. Sir HENRY NORMAN Will probably replY that, even if he does not take part in nearlY so many divisions as Mr. BYLES, he is never to be found in the Opposition lobby. He does not vote "on his own." He does not rcaka *
I

- special display of sympathy with the Labour party by voting against a Front Bench which js . --- doing all that it possibly can for labour. Mr. BYLEB suggests that he must therefore be for "the .2 Government, right or wrong." But neither does this follow from Sir HENRY Nohmier's argument • which, if it must be admitted, is one that it is • difficult to maintain. Even the most loyal of -Parliamentarians must be left in possession of some amount of private judgment,—ih the . Liberal party at least. The question, we take it, entirely resolves itself . Into a matter of general principles. If a member 'supporta the principles of a measure like, for example, the Old Age Pensions Bill, how far is he justified in voting in favour of any alteration , in its details ? Sir Henry Norman will scarcely . contend, we believe, that any of the offending members have gone further than that. For his 1. k own part he takes the word of Ministers and of the Ministerial Whips that all possible concessions have been made. He does not vote, therefore, on the -ground of what he would like—that is of what he "thinks right "—but he votes for a 1-- Government which is doing all it can. Here is a 0 ' fine problem in casuistry, it must be admitted. , Why should a private member be expected to -vote against what he thinks right? The question) we must again point out, only applies to matters ofsletail. Voting according toMr.BYLES'S notions of Parliamentary freedom means putting the Government into a difficulty concerning minor .. points of Bills, the general principle of which has been affirmed even by those who oppose the Government on details. We should not be for making discipline too rigid in circumstances of that description. Undoubtedly, however, there is a danger of defeating tho Ministry without intending to do . an, and although the conditions of the defeat might not involve the resignation of the Ministry,

'they might be so often repeated as to indnce the Ministry to resign. That is just what happened in 1895. Too much independence on the part of certain Liberal members drove the Government to the resolution to resign office on an adverse vote
in Committee. There has seldom been a change of Government so unfortunate in its 'consequences,

among which was the Boer War. The same kind of thing may happen again under similar con- ditions of surprise. It would be :well, therefore, in our opinion, for members like Mr. BYLES to oposider the question of independent voting in • o3ntection with the possibility of defeating a Government which they would beyond all things desire to keep in power.

We heartily congratulate • THE 'MAarsraerEs the police on having AND LICENSING brought a charge against PaosEcurioNs. a local licensee for serving a drunken man with beer, and we svmpathise with thorn on the abortive result of the prosecution. There is not the least doubt that drunken men are served with drink by the publicans every night that passes, or we should not sae so much drunkenness in the streets. But however desirous the police are of • doing theff dety,they are practically helpless unless - they have the support and encouragement of both Watch Committee and magistrates. Unfortunately aome of our J.P's are not free from the suspicion of Putting the interests of the brewers before those of the town and the public. On Monday, in the • prosecution under notice, the police evidence was Cl. that a drunken man had been served with drink, yet the magistrates by a majority of five to - four decided to dismiss the defendant on payment of costs. " They considered a technical offence had been committed" said the Mayor" and that , the Police were perfectly justified in bringing the he before them." If serving a drunken man can I,rie passed over as a technical offence we wonder ,flow far the publican may go in defiance of the 'aw withont having a conviction rqcorded against him. We are sick and tired of these wishy-washy verdicts of " guilty, but don't 'do it again." The police ought to have the fullest Support in such cases, and the Bench onght to err . on the aide of severity rather than leniency in the s 'lnterests not only of the town, but of the publicans themselves. The administration of the licensing hats in Warringtnn is deplorably slack and -,,verdicts of this kind are the despair of temperance ;reformers. To all intents and purposes they give the publican—generally a tied•house tenant—eirte blanche to do as he likes in squeezing out such a profit as will satisfy the brewer. It amounts to that the brewer is more feared than the 13ench

The advisability of taking ADVEETISTIsiG steps to advertise Warring- Waunrsanor ton as a commercial and manufacturing centre has been urged more than once in the Council chamber, usually by Councillor Pemberton, So far as we know, nothing has been done in this direction. Now is the time when it should once More be brought before the notice of our muni- cipal administrators. The new Patents Act is certain to result in a large amount of foreign capital being transferred to England for the pur- pose of manufacturing on the spot articles . Pr.eviously "made in Germany" or else- where abroad. Foreign manufacturers are already taking steps to overcome the difficulty , 'With which they are faced, and judicious adver- tising might conceivably 'result in some the more enterprising firms being attracted to ' Warrington. The question has already been . considered by the St. Helens Council, and what 'vould be good for St. Helens in this case would U 9 much better for Warrington considering our s.uperior facilities for rail and water transport. It • _ a question whether the town could legitimately ; employ an agent to push its claims, but there is certainly a real necessity for advertising in some ' form or other, and we hope the Council will - show themselves wide awake to the possibilities stretched out invitingly before their gaze. -- ' To see ourselves as others - As Onnos SEE S. see us is interesting and gt sometimes profitable. The anchester City News" has been devoting a couple of columns to an article on "Warrington , cl,f all Trades," which is pleasantly written and uescribem many things as they are—from the trout nursery in the Park to sanitation needs—but afters little in the way of instructive criticism. , I -khere is, perhaps, most interest for Warrington pteople in the first paragraph of the article, since Opens by saying: . " Warrington is essentially a Cheshire town, though from a mere geographical point of view , it lies partly in Lancashire. Its older streets, I winding between buildings of a dull rel brick 1 picturesquely varied, now and then, by a bit of I lack and white architecture with a history, I remind you somewhat of rinutsford, somewhat of Chester:" i 1 ft„. , vi -Lois s amusing. We never looked upon War- t orzton as a Cheshire town before, but rather as • Zpical of Lancashire and Lancashire industry. _pother reference to Warrington is " Cranford, I,,wltb a difference "—which is distinctly flattering! 4 •• Pend. I l ~. "On a sunny forenoon, lounging in the winding • thoroughfares among the respectably solid-looking -.-. t stills. J t b you are reminded of Cranford by the ill ougbam which stops at a draper's door. It has no occupant, but John, I the dignified coachman, hands down a shred of ribbon to the shop assistant. He has been sent to" town" to match it for Miss Susie, who is • eking some dainty trifle for the church t, -v,',gazaar." 1.- tt, that a sleepy hollow we are vegetating in, to • I,l_llre. However, 'tis pleasant to meet with a - -'"ger who can see something in the old town VI,

other than black smoke and abominable pavements. The writer of the article wakens a little later on, and begins to talk of wire, engines, tubes, ele and soap—which are the more striking concomitants of life in Warrington. "Its Gouncil to-day I bel'eve, is above reproach"he says,"and without desiring to rummage amongst any causes of criticism in the past, it must be said that the sarre statement couli not truly be made half a score of years ay." Wtl wonder if he got this information at the Town Hall, which was among the places the writer visited in the course of his bird's-eye view I One discovery he made was that " gas is cheap." Evidently it is all a matter of comparison. After a reference to our antiquated sewage system, and the need for a public abattoir, he concludes with a complimentary personal note (accompanied by fairly faithful portraits) on the Mayor and the Town Clerk.

div.head: TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: TOWN COUNCIL.
Business of Tuesday's Meeting.
The monthly meeting of the Town Council will be held on Tuesday, when the following other .business will be transacted.
SPECIAL MOTIONS.

_ 1, Alderman Ellison will move that the control and management of the Old Warps Estate be vested in the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee. 2, Councillor Pemberton will move (I) that a com- mittee be appointed, called the "Towns Committee." (2) that a sum of £5O be granted to the Towns Com- mittee forthwith. IDF.NING or WILDERS POOL _CAUSEWAY.

The Street Improvement Committee lias resolved: After further consideration of the offer of George Artingstall and Co., Ltd., for the sale of the front of their premises in Wilderspool Causeway, it was decided not to entertain the same. mussrts. MILLING'S SKY SIGN. The Town Clerk reported that Messrs. Henry Milling and Co., Ltd., had erected a sky sign over their premises in Horsemarket-street contrary to the Warrington Corporation Act of 1899 : Resolved, that no sky sign be allowed in• the Borough, and that Messrs. Henry Milling and Co., be served with notice to remove the sign erected by them. NEW ASSISTANT MEDICAL OFFICEIt. _ _ _ . .

The Health Committee had resolved that Dr. Claude Van Buren be appointed assistant medical officer of health at a salary of £250 per annum. The latter's resignation was subsequently received and the position again advertised.

div.head: PUBLIC ABATTOIR..
div.p: PUBLIC ABATTOIR..

A discussion took place in the Health Committee on the advisability of establishing a public abattoir, and after considering the views expressed by the sub-com- mittee who were appointed to report on the matter, it was resolved that, providing the owners of slauFhter- houses in the borough will carry out the conditions required by the Medical Officer of Health for the alteration and improvement of such slaughter-houses, the time is-not opportune for tho establishment of a public abbatoir. At a later meeting the Afedical 03cer of Health sub- mitted his recommendations with regard to the cleansing of slaughter-houses in the borough, and it was resolved, that a copy be sent to the Butcher's Association with an intimation that the Committee'are prepared to meet them for the purpose of discussing the matter.

div.head: PRICE OF OAS.
div.p: PRICE OF OAS.

At a meeting of tl;e7-6-tia-00-ainiittee, a letter from the Warrington Tradesmen's Association was read requesting a reduction in the price of gas, and the Town Clerk reported that he had informed the Association that the question was already under consideration. ELECTRICITY AND TRAMWAYS. The above committee resolved that the charge of the car sheds, upkeep of the cars, and the engineering work connected therewith, and the control of the men employed on the work be transferred to the Tramways Manager without any increase of salary for six months. Resolved that the salary of the Engineer remain as at present. Resolved, that Mr. IT. 13. Jackson be appointed Chief Assistant Engineer at a stlary of £153 per annum. Resolved, that Mr. F. V. Jordan be appointed Maine Engineer at the salary of £l3O per annum, rising by £lO per annum to a mesimam of £l5O. The Committee in making the above alterations in the duties of the Engineer, hive done so in order to keep the two departments as far as ,possible distinct, and no reflection is cast upon Mr. 'Mathias who has hitherto discharged the duties to the entire satisfaction of the Committee.

ALLOTMENTS. The following applications for allotments have been granted :—John 'Wood, 40, Monks-street, acre; Thomas Drury, 5,3, Cumberland-street, acre; T. Broomball, 25, Slater-street, acre; James Rowe, 13, Belmont Avenue I acre; William Miller, 3, Brook Place, acre; Thomas Hewitt, 4, Hewitt-street, acre; resolved that consent be given to the transfer of Allotment No. 11 from Mr. G. W. R. Baines, to Mr. Thomas Taylor.

OPEN SPACES AND DOWLING GREENS. The General Purposes Committee has resolved, that the following recommendations of the Open Spaces Sub-committee be approved and adopted:—" Resolved: That the General Purpose Committee be recommended to calse the Liverpool-road Recreation Ground to be levelled, the railings surrounding the same to be repaired, and posts to be erected to prevent carts from crossing the grotmd. And "Resolved : That the committee be recommended to proceed with the con- struction of a bowling green there." The following resolution of the Open Spaces Sub- committee was read :—" Resolved: Mat the com- mittee be recommended to erect a fence on the southern boundary of tile land in St. Elphin's Park, Manchester- road, and the land thrown open to the public." Resolved, that the land be handed over to the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee and that they be requested to prepare plan and estimate for the laying out of the land.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

One of the most expert conjurors who have ever visited Warrington is to be seen at the Hippodrome this week in the person of Hermann Melot, a French- man. His display has aroused the liveliest interest at every performance. We have never seen a conjuror do more with a bowler hat. From it he produced buttonholes, cigarettes, etc. by the bushel, and threw them among the audience. There seemed to be an endless supply in that empty hat, and when he had got tired of producing the flowers, Mons. Melot brought two or three fluttering doves from the same uncommon cage. Another little feat was to break and empty an egg into the hat and a moment later extract the egg whole again. Finally the hat went back to the owner seemingly none the worse and not a bit mysterious. There were other clever feats in the Frenchman's repertoire but we have not space to detail them. He must be seen to be appre- ciated. Virto is one of those fantastic musicians who give selections on various wierd instruments. His turn was loudly encored, but why the performer should appear in a billiard cloth green frock suit with white spats and white waistcoat is " one of those things no feller can understand." Virto would have looked nicer in black. A unique speciality act, "The Tramp in the Nursery " is given by the Forsyths. The "tramp " discovers a life-size animated doll in the "nursery" and sets it to work. Of course, the doll is real live,and we have nothing but the highest praise for the skill of the lady who takes the role of " la poupee." Fine fun is provided lay Mr. J. Gar Kiddie and his troupe in the absurdity" The House of Tinn." A mad pace is set from the start and the frolic keeps everybody laughing. Mr. Kiddie is very droll as " one o' the lads," and a good word should be said Tor Mr. J. W. Groves as Mrs. Tinn, and for Miss Lizzie Payne and the other dancing girls. Most of us have tried a little shadowgraphy on the blind at some time Or other, but Chassino has raised this simple amuse- ment to an art. Some of the caricatures he shadows on the screen with both hands and feet are wonderfully good, and indicate uncommon expertness. C,hassino also does a little whistling of a high order. " Mr. E." has a series of pictures about which be patters more or less humorously, the Evalos do some jocular jugglery, and the Sisters Varier appear with success as duettists. The bio-tableaux firings a very entertain- ing programme to a close after a full two hours.

div.head: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.
div.p: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.

Next week the star turn will be provided by May Moor-Duprez, the jolly Dutch girl who will appear iu her latest successes. The Kirbys, the popular comedy and burlesque entertainers, are sure to be a great attraction. In addition the following artistes will contribute to a capital programme :—George Lawrence, light comedian; San Remo Girls, come- diennes and dancers; Kremka Bros., comedy acrobats; the Four Maisanos, eccentric musicians; Erne , Reynolds, the well known London vocalist; the Fire ' Bombays, harmony singers and speciality dancers.

div.head: SPECIAL MATINEE.
div.p: SPECIAL MATINEE.

We would call the attention of our readers to the fact that a special matinee in aid of the staff outing will be held next Thursday. A splendid programme has been arranged and we are sure the patrons of the Palace will show their appreciation of the uniform oourtesy of the staff by attending in large numbers.
The Examiner, Saturday, July 4, 1908.

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.

Liverpool-road recreatiot ground is to be immedi- ately put in order, and steps taken for laying the second municipal bowling green there. Up to now the recreation ground has been more like unto a rubbish-tip than anything else. * * * Mr. and Mrs. A. H. Crostield were in Warrington yesterday and witnessed the Walking Day processions. Afterwards they visited the Infirmary and were con- ducted through the various wards. * * * Congratulations to Major J. Dutton Fairclough on his appointment as lioutenant.colonel of the local Volunteer Battalion. He is a capable and enthusiastic officer and has well earned his promotion to the leadership of the corps. * * * The dignity of such an important body as the Stockton Heath Parish Council is not proof against the heat and on Tuesd ty evening there was no pro- test when M. H. J. Westbrook laid aside his coal before presiding over the meeting. Even Stockton Heath Parish Councillors are human ! •* * * Nesr.hats were 4e rigeur on Walking Day, and even the Borough police followed the dictates of fashion. They walked about with an air of conscious pride, resplendent in brand new straw helmets. The innovation is an admirable -one in all respects. Policemen, above all others, should have cool heads!

* * * Teeslay was the list day on which Volunteers could join the new Territorial Force for twelve months only. AU euliAing nov will have to under- tau toprve four years. The strength of the 4th V.B. South Lancashire Regiment is now 694. The estabLehment bf the battalion is fixed at 1009 so that there is plenty of roam for more.

•I * Mr. John Ward, M.P., who is secretary of the Navvies' Union, has been invited to be present at the opening of the Bristol ducks by the King on the 9th July, and he has accepted the invitation, This is the first time that such a compliment has been extended to the official representative o the mum. In this case, at least, the policy of their exclusion has not been followed.

* * * ' Many people were surprised when they saw Messrs. Milling's huge new eky-sign ia press of erection, for such thingsare usually. "taboo" in progressive municipalities. The sign ies a fine one from an advertising point of view, but we doubt whether any per.ons not members of the firm view it with pleasure when walking up Bridge-street. Anyhow, the sky- sign has to c me down as it is contrary to the War- rington Corporation Act of 1899. * * . .

The news that a footbri.age over the river between Howley and Victoria Park is to be proceeded with immediately, comes as a bombshell. After the scheme and the coutract have passed the Council we are told that the work will be completed in six weeks. Let us hope so, but after the lingering f Ate of Warrington Bridge one cannot help feeling sceptical. By the way, we presume the cyclist will be able to take his machine over the new structure. * *

"Really, you know nothing about it—you only think you do," said Jr. Will Crooks, M.P., speaking in favour of the Eight Hours Bill, at the annual de.nonstration of the North Staffordshire Miners' Federation held recently at Trenthom Park. " You have not been to the right school," he continued ;"you . have only been to the school where they-get the coal, not to the school ;There they get all the oof out of it." (Laughter.) The arguments against the- Bill in the House of Commons he described as the most "paralys- ing piffle" he ever heard. " What is all the world to a man if his wife's a widow ? " (Laughter.) * * * Those who attended tha prize distribution at the Training College on Saturday were mach impressed by the practical and high toned address of the Lord Mayor of Liverpool. He gave some capital advice to the future teachers, not the least important being his advocacy of the teaching of the evils of alcohol. We are glad to think that instruction in temperance has made great progress in the schools of late years— thanks largely to the-energetic work of the Band of Rope Union —but it would be a great gain if the subject could be made a permanent part of the curriculum.

* * Definitions of drunkenness are continually being added to, but they do not contribute much to the general enlightenment. Not long since Dr. Fox said it was possible for a man to be drunk in his legs and not in his head. Whichever end wobbled we should think he was drunk. But a defendant at Birkenhead the other day went further than the Doctor and said "A man is not drunk till he goas to the punapto light his pipe." Judging by the number of prosecutions for drunkenness in Warrington we should think the latter is the definition acted upon in Warrington. * * *

The following nine magistrates adjudicated oa Monday on a prosecution for serving a drunken man with drink —The Mayor, Alderman Tinnion, Cata- cillor Wilkinson, Councillor J. Evans, Mr. C. J. Holmes, Mr. S. Wright, Mr. G. Pilling, Mr. W. Itobc..rts and Mr. W. Furness. The offence was proved, the Bench described it as a technical offence, and the case was dismissed oa payment of costs. If this was a " tecunical "offence, what is a real punishable offence in the view of these worthy J.P.'s ? We are informed that four of the nine voted for a conviction, bet the remaining five carried the day. Problem :—Who are the four staunch friends of temperance who believed that a breach of the Licensing Laws should be followed by a penalty? Perhaps they will write and tell us! * * * Though the public has never .been informed who was responsible for the lax state of things which culminated in the tragedy of Mr. 11. P. Brierley's suicide, it will be interesting news to many that a new system of keeping Corporation stores has been devised and comes into operation with the Ist of this month. There was an investigation into the condition cf things after the Briarley affair, and full information was promised the Council; but the report of the Investigation Committee has never made its appear- ance, unless possibly it appeared in camera. The matter has been skilfully and successfully shelvecl,and it is not, perhaps, worth while re-opening it now, but there was at the time a strong public demand for the fullest particulars which should certainly have been complied with even if some reputations suffered thereby. As the stable-door is now locked we are not disposed to peep through the key daole !

Lord Shuttle worth, who has been appointed to succeed the late Earl of Derby as Lord-Lieutenant of Lancashire, will be best remembered by most as Sir 11gbtred Kay-Shuttlewortb, son of the first Secretary to the Board of Education, and himself Secretary t) the Admiralty during Mr. Gladstono's fourth adminis- tration and during Lord Rosebery's Premiership. He made his first appearance at St. Stephen's nearly 40 years ago, representing Hastinzs until 1830, and the Clitheroo Division of Lancashire from 188.5 until he was created first Baron Shattleworth in 1902. He is the owner of some 4,000 or 5,000 acres, and the author of a book entitled The First Principles of Modern Chemistry" for in his London University days he had decided upon chemistry as-a career, politics being an afterthought. A strong Churchman, though a Radical, he has been described as one of the best Chairmen of Committees the House of Commons ever had. He married in 1371 a daughter of Sir Woodbine Parish, himself a remarkable man of many achievements.

** * 1 The local Tariff Reformers were evidently much impressed by the. success of the outdoor meetings of the Progressive Labour League—for last Monday they followed suit. But what 3 marked difference between , the political matter before the audiences ! On the one ' hand the speakers attached to the Progressive Labour League brought out solid facts —substantiated by Blue Books and other weighty authorities, in support of their case. Whereas on the other hand the would-be Tariff Reformers tried to build up their case on.a foundation of sand, which naturally on examination crumbles away. Take Councillor Broadhurst 's , speech for example. He criticised the speeches which had been made during the previous week by Messrs. Howes, England and Elwell on Germany, and held up the latter country as an example to ours. Oar contemporary, the " neutral" organ, has been unkind enough—no doubt quite unintentionaly to shatter his whole argument, for it has published a summary of the Report issued last Friday by the Board of Trade on the condition of things in Germany. The article is headed:—
COST OF LIVING IN GERMANY. COMPARISONS 'WITH THE UNITED KiNanom.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
Second Week of Mr. Ryder Boys'
Season.

Mr. Ryder Boys' Company complete the second week of their stay here this (Saturday) evening. The long spell of glorious summer weather has had its effect on the attendances at the theatre, but those who have witnessed any of this week's performances have been delighted with the high-class productions of this very talented company. On Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday evenings, the attraction was the Nihilist dratna "The Red Lamp" by W. Ontram-Tristram, which has found a place in the repertoire of that great actor, Mr. H. Beerbohm Tree. It is a thrilling play giving an insight into the anarchy and tyranny which unhappily loom so large in the history of Russia. We hear of plots against the Czar's life, and ceaseless raids on th• Nihilists, and the atmosphere is heavy with conspiracy and intrigue. The most notable feature of the drama is the remarkable character study associ- ated with the part of Paul Demetrius; of the Secret Police. He is one of those inscrutable men,apparently inoffensive yet always compassing somebody's down- fall, and his appearance presages trouble. Mr. William Calvert's portrayal was a masterly one and roused the audiences to enthusiasm. His make-up was perfect and throughout he maintained that insinuating, imperturbable demeanour which puzzles everyone. Miss Alice Hughes as Princess Claudia Valerian distinguished herself with powerful. dramatic acting, and made the most of several highly emotional scenes in which she played a leading part. Miss Ethel Norbury was a winsome Olga, and Miss Betty Noel was artless and artful as Felise. Mr. Leonard Afudie was well placed as Prince Alexis Valerian, who joins the Nihilists, and his passionate declarations of faith in the cause were finely delivered. Mr. Henry Worrell, too, rose to the occasion as Ivan Zazzulic, whose treachery has such an import• ant bearing on the story, and Mr. Murray Graham did particularly well as Allan Villiers, the cute American journalist. Mr. Harold Neville presented a capital study of General Morakoff and Mr. Allan Mudie as Kertch, was the personification of enforced servility, combined with a loathing of society. The minor parts were in capable bands and the play held the unflagg- ing interest of the audience from beginning to end. On Thursday evening there was a change in the programme, that well-known favourite with theatre goers, "The Robbery of the Lyons Mail," in which the late Sir Henry Irving used to achieve such triumphs, being presented. It is possible also to speak in the highest terms of this performance, special credit being due to Mr. Henry Worrell, who excelled himself in the dual role of Lesurques and Dubose. Our readers could not do better than see the con- cluding performance of "The Lyons Mail" this [Saturday) evening. They will certainly be well repaid-

div.head: NEXT WEEK'S PROGIUDIME.
div.p: NEXT WEEK'S PROGIUDIME.

Mr. Ryder Boys' Company will again occupy the boards nest week cvhen a repertoire of special interest will be submitted. On Monday, Tuesday and Saturday evenings the attraction will be the ever popular play by Lord Lytton, " The Lady of Lyons." -Mr. Henry Worrell will appear as Claude and Missalice Hughes as Pauline. Thursday will be a special nigltt, when Warringtonians will have the opportunity of seeing Mr. Ryder Boys as Hardcastle in " She Stoops to Conquer." Mr. Ryder Boys is famous in Manchester for his many interesting revivals at the Princes' and Queen's Theatres, and has played in Mr. Flanagan's big productions of Macbeth, the first part of Henry IV. and Antony and Cleopatra. He is very highly esteemed in his adopted city, and his performances are one of the most interesting events of the season. Hardcastle is one of his best performances. On Wednesday and Friday the Company will present the great drama " A. Fool's Paradise," as played by Sir John Hare, Mr. Harold Neville will appear as Sir Peter Lund and Miss Ethel Norbury as Beatrice Selwyn.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
RUNCORN WOMAN'S THEFTS.

At Runcorn, on Monday, an elderly— ;•O-lan named Sarah Crompton pleaded guilty to stealing Ll 10s. sd. belonging to her nephew, Edward Rarnsden, of Sewell- street, Runcorn. She took the money from a cashbox , on the kitchen dresser. She told the bench she expected ! to be able to place the money back before the theft VMS discovered.—A fine of 30s. or fourteen days was imposed. I SUPPOSED SUICIDE AT RUNCORN. • I About mindight on Thursday Sarah Crompton (47) , was seen hurrying along tho bank of a big pool con- nected with the Bridgewater Canal at Runcorn. Then ! there were cries of " Help." In twenty minutes John ! Ratcliffe recovered the body with a boat hook. Artificial respiration was tried without effect. The deceased was on Monday convicted of robbing her nephew, and it is believed she committed suicide. She would have to clear a rail to reach the water. MARRIAGE OF MR. M. E. LOUIS BUCKLEY.

St. Mary's Church, Sandown-park, Wavertree, was the scene of a picturesque wedding on Tuesday, when Miss Beatrice Marner-Smvthe, of Bantallard,' Wavertree, was married to Mr. -Marcus E. Louis Buckley, son of Mr. John Buckley, Runcorn. The church was prettily decorated with masses of cool green ferns and palms in the chancel, and white flowers on the Communion table. An organ recital was given by Mr. F. R. Borastoo, organist of the Parish Church. Runcorn during the arrival of the guests and after the ceremony. The service was fully choral, and began with the hymn " The Voice that breathed o'er Edeu," and concluded with "0 perfect love." The officiating clergy were the Von. Archdeacon Madden, the Rev. Louis IL Smythe (brother of the bride), the Rev. J. T. Mitchell (rector of tV'avertree), the Rev. P. Latimer Davies (vicar of St. James's, Liverpool), and the Rev. W. A. Scholes (Runcorn.) De. J. Leabury Smythe (brother of the bride) accompanied the bridegroom as best man._

The bride, who was given away by her father, was a dainty picture in ivory satin and lace. The gown was made Empire style, with a long train lined with glace silk and adorned with a horseshoe of orange blossom. The cream-tinted,Maltese lace that bordered the train and draped the bodice was the gift of Mrs. Weissenberg. A tiara of orange blossom was worn under the long I tulle veil, and the bridal boupet was of whito roses I and lilies.

The trio of pretty bridesmaids were Miss Lucie Marner-Smythe (sister of the bride), Miss May Weissenberg, and Miss Jeanie Dron. They wore charm- ing frocks of turquoise blue taffetas, cut en princesse, with transparent yokes and sleeves of spotted net and lace motifs. Their large crinoline hats were swathed with tulle and blue ribbon, and finished with clusters of pink reses.The bridegroom gave them shower bouquets of La France roses and gold pendant brooches set with pearls and emeralds.

After the ceremony a reception was held at the resi- dence of the bride's parents, where numerous beautiful presents were on view. Ur. and Mrs. Marcus E. Louis Buckley started early in the afternoon for North %Vales,where the honeymoon is to be passed. The bride looked charming in her travelling costume of cream serge, trimmed with military braid and gold buttons, and a becoming hat of poppy red straw and choux of red ribbon.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
PIT CAGE TIZAGEDY.

Michael Murphy, aged thirty-two, Parr, met with.= extraordinary death on Monday night, at the Ash ton's Green Colliery, St. Helens. He was going with two other men to work. His companions got into the cage at the top of the pit shaft, but when he attempted to enter, the cage began to descend. Murphy tried to draw back, but failed, and fell bait-way into the cage, and was crushed between the top of the cage and landing plate, and instantly killed. ST, HELENS AND NON-UNION MINERS.

The miners employed at the Ashton's Green Colliery last week followed the example set them some time ago by the men at the Havannah Colliery, near, by giving notice to strike in order to compel the non-union men who are employed at the pit to join the Miners' Federa- tion. It was stated that about 100 men refused to join the union, but since notices to stop work were handed in the bulk of the non-union men have taken up mem- bership, and it is most unlikely that any stoppage will take place.

div.head: 'DRUNKEN COLLIERS' ESCAPADE.
div.p: 'DRUNKEN COLLIERS' ESCAPADE.

• Thomas 0 reeuall, Talbot-street, and Samuel Critchley, Silver-street, looked very foolish when charged at St. tielens on Monday, with lodging out and committing wilful damage to a window.—Police-constable Bradley said that soon after Saturday night be found the panes of glass and the window-sash at 61, -Hack Water-street were broken. On getting through the window he went upstairs, and found the two men, who are colliers, asleep on the bedroom floor. Greenall was very drunk and had to be carried downstairs and lifted bodily through the window. When charged, he said" If i was in the house someone must have thrown me through the window." The magistrates sent the men to gaol for twenty-one days for lodging out, and ordered them to pay Ills, for the damage.
THE BETTING NUISANCE. ST. HELENS MEN SNIARTLY FINED.

Seventeen charges of street betting and helping Lookmakers were down for trial at St. Helens Police Court on Monday. Thomas Kelly, Campbell-street, and William Glynn. Kirkland-street, were first charged with betting in a passage between Banner-street and Crispin-street, on June 17.

Inspector Sisson said that Kelly was employed by a firm of bookmakers, but Glynn made a book on his own account. The passage was occasionally crowded with people. Kelly was in full view, and they saw him take bets from 157 men, eighty-one women, twenty-five boas, and eight girls, a total of 271. Glynn denied the offence, and called a young man named Fairhurst, who swore that on this date they were in company with another man seeking work at Collins Green and Sutton Heath Pits.

_ Glynn admitted that he had lost a lot of money on , betting, but produced nawntickets and a book referring to a loan to show that he was hard up, and not able to bet with anybody. , Sergeant Ackers spoke to seeing Kelly and Glynn ! betting on this day, and said that William Kay came to Kelly and collected the betting slips and money. Mr. E. W. Swift defended Key, and cross-examined to show that he carried on a legitimate and regular business as a hairdresser. He contended that the one incident spoken to by the police did not constitute the offence of 'frequenting." Kelly was charged on thre,o summonses and William Glynn three ; William Kay, Duke-street, two charges ; Samuel Kay, jun. Gresswell-street, one charge. Thomas Glynn, of Havelock-street ; John Wilson, 97, Lyon- street ; and James Leach, 42, Duncan-street, were charged with aiding and abetting. William Smith, Newton-road, and Thomas Smith, Newton-road, were charged with street betting ; and John Shaw and Thomas Smith were summoned for aid- ing and abetting. ! Thomas Kelly was fined in three cases a total of £3O or six months. Glynn was also fined in three cases £3O lor six months. William Kay was fined £lO or two ! months. Thomas Glynn, John Wilson, and James Leech were each fined £lO or two months for aiding and I abetting. I In the cases of William and Thomas Smith, and a man named Ward, Mr. Swift defended, and the magis- trates fined NVilliam Smith £lO on each of the two !charges, and dismissed the other cases.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
ANOTHER COAL THEFT.

Mary Davies, a young woman from Burtonwood, was charged at Newton, with stealing 50lbs. of coal, worth 21d., from the Collins Green Colliery Co.—Mr. Peace, for the Company, said they were obliged to prosecute, to stop the pilfering of coal continually going on at their sidings.—P.C. Georgeson deposed to finding the young woman in the act of taking the coal at 6 o'clock in the morning.—Defendant said her husband had been out of work, had justod started work that morning, but had not drawn anything. They had only been married three months.—The Clerk : You don't seem to realize what a serious thing this is, and that you might be scut to prison.—Fived 10s. including costs.

wards sold it to another man for 103., which however, he had not received.—P.O. Ileath said that upon information he charged the prisoner with stealing the bicycle, which he admitted, and told witness be had sole it at Runcorn. The prisoner, whose parents live at Salford, had been to sea, but was out of work and on tramp when he stole the bicycle. The Chairman said the prisoner had been bound over four times already, after committing petty thefts, and it was no use binding him over again. He would have to go to prison for two months.

WIFE DESERTION AND CRUELTY AT EARLESTOWN. At the Newton Petty Sessions last Thursday, before Col. Wood (chairman), Messrs. F. Wood, E. T. Evans, and W. Collingwood, John Davies, of Earlestown, was charged by his wife, Mary J. Davies, with deserting her.—Detendant at (kat admitted the charge, but then denied it, saying he was turned out. He could not afford to pay more than Bs. a week, having a brother and sister to look after.—The Clerk: Your wife and children must be looked after before them.—The wife said she would rather go to the Workhouse than live with him again.—lnspector lanes and Sergeant Cooper said they had had complaints from the woman about her husband's treatment, and they found him a most violent tempered and foul-mouthed. Man.—The Bench made an order for separation and payment of 10s. a week, the Clerk suggesting the Police Court Missionary might use his good offices to bring abopt a better understand- ing between the parties. James MeGrail, of Earlestown, appeared to answer an adjourned charge of persistent cruelty to his wif Mary A. McGrail.—Mrs. McGrail gave evidence of he husband's drunkenness, foul language, and assaults. He son had taken a knife from him when he was threatenin her. She had two young children, beside others grow e up. Her husband had earned about £2 a week as collier, but having had an accident he had recentl been taking club money and compensation amounting to about 265. a week. He had been fined 26 times for drunkenness, and she and the family had to suffer all the while through it.—P.-Sergt. Cooper deposed to being called by the complainant, and found the man drunk, violent, and using very bad lan.nage.—James McGrail, a son of the parties, said that had been the sort of conduct his father had been guilty of as long as ,he could remember. He had taken a knife out of his hand, and had many times interfered between them.-- ! Defendant said they all wanted to get shut of hirs because he was nearly past woik.—Mr. Hudson, Police Court Missionary, said he had failed to do any good I between the parties, and the defendant would make no offer.—Order made for separation and payment of Ds, a week.

div.head: BAYDOCK FIREMAN'S FATAL HURRY.
div.p: BAYDOCK FIREMAN'S FATAL HURRY.

Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy coroner, held an inquest on Tuesday afternoon at Ilaydock on Robert Smith (57), colliery fireman, of 54, Judfleld St. Ha had worked at Pewfall Colliery for ten years. He went on work on Sunday afternoon, the 14th ult. A big fall took place in the lower motion brow, and deceased spoke to his men across the fall,and then started to go to them over the fall. Whoa he got to the other side he fell. He was removed to hospital where he died. Mr. Hall said the accident seemed to be due due to hurry. The man had climbed over the fall and the stones had slipped from under him, and ho fell about nine feet on to the rails. It was unfortunate that a fireman who was always so careful should meet with his end in this way.—A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

SENT TO GAOL FOIL STEALING A BICYCLE. John Lydiat, of Runcorn, pleaded guilty at Newton Sessions last Thursday, to stealing a bicycle. worth 305., the property of Ernest Unsworth, licensee of the Boat- house public house, Itiston, on June 2nd. Prosecutor said he remembered the prisoner calling at the house with another young man, and at closing time they asked to be allowed to sleep in the stable. He agreed, and locked them in, but in the morning they were gone, and so was the bicycle.—lsaao Tease, of Runcorn, said he bought the bicycle from the defendant, who seemed to give a reasonable account of it, and he believed it was his own. A TEACHER lately, wishing to turn the young ides towards the mission field, asked : " What are good men called who leave their homes and go to foreign lands to teach the heathen?" " Prodigal sons," was the prompt and triumphant reply. A class of boys when asked "What were the ten plagues ?" answered, with more fervour than gallantry, "'The ten virgins, Si?."

"To tell the truth, she had on such a lovely pink blouse that I didn't hear a word she said."
