impressed on telegraph clerks and Priniers, that in this case "Antony" has no "h." Bat apart from that flippant reason, Sir Antony's elevation is to be welcomed because he is at last Unmuzzled," as Mr. etladstoue said when he was freed from the repre- sentation of Oxford. lie has remained very faithful to the traditions of the civil service in keeping silence on many an occasion when his name was the sport of politicians. Be will now be able to express his personal opinions on the government. of Ireland— advanced and enlightened opinions they are —in the House of Parliament where they can be expressed to most advantage, and where hitherto generous ideas in regard to Ireland have been vastly overpowered by the angry cry of irreconcilable landlords. On Indian questions, too, the new Peer's opinions will be of great interest and value. LORDS CCTRZO AND MIDLETOSI. There was a very fine debate in the House of Lords this week, showing how much the Peers have grine:l by the translation of Mr. John Morley, and his trans- ' formation into Viscount Morley of Blackburn. There is another strong man who has recently crept into that House as a representative Irish Peer, Lord Citizen of Kedleston, the late Indian Viceroy! He has an almost overpowering personality, due to his great industry, ability,end fluency of speech,and unbounded self-confidence ; and there is a third comparatively new Peer, Viscount Midleton, who, as Mr. Brodrick, was Secretary of State for India during part of Lord Curzon's Viceroyalty, and had a memorable passage- at-arms in dispatches with his brilliant subordinate,in which he was backed up by the Tory Government' The consequence was that Lord Curzon came back with, as was supposed, no great love for the men with whom he now associates and rather outshines on the front Opposition bench of the House of Lords, and, at all events, no great affection for Lord- Midleton. The explosion at the contact of these two clouded tempers has been looked for ever since Lord Curzon came into the House, but it did not actually occur until Tuesday. It was no great affair even then. LORD MORLEY'S LESSON TO LORD CURZON. The debate was really memorable for the lesson given by Viscount Morley to the late Viceroy, and for the fine political wiedom as well as the accustomed literary grac:§ewhicri adorned Lord Morley's speech. Lord Curzon sneers at House of Commons questions concerning Indian affairs, and other signs of a certain nnoonscions arrogance, culminating in a lecture to i Lord Morley on the way in which he should carry on ' British traditional policy in India, procured from the Indian Secretary a reply full of dignity, and at the ' same time of remorseless exposure of his outwardly polite but essentially impertinent assailant's defects of temper and statesmanship. Lord Curzon bad betrayed great sensitiveness as to the effect of Lord Middleton's telegram on Indian opinion of himself, be had dwelt mach on the effects caused in "the whispering galleries of the East," by what was said and done in other parts of the world; but he was blind to the bearing of his own words on this theory of Eastern dangers. Lord Morley opened his eyes, and gave him back in language even more picturesque than his own the retort that there were listeners in the fastnesses of Kabul to what had been said about the Ameer, and that his language on the Indian :situation would be regarded, by men "who are looking on our, Govern- ment with a sinisieigleam in their eyes and infatuated dreams in their hearts," as helpful to them. It was amusinr, to note Lord Curzon's surprise at being accused of making a party speech. He was perfectly unconscious, as these returned Pro-consuls who rejoin their Party in Parliament so often are, that he had taken on the manners of a Party man. The impres- sion is that Lord Curzon on Tuesday night had been helped to find his Parliamentary level, and that less will be heard of him in the immediate future. The Rediotelegraphie Convention having been signed by the British Government, the Great Eastern Railway Company decided to fit their steamers with a system of wireless telegraphy, and two of the boats on the Hook of Holland service, the Turbine steamer Copenhagen, and the twin screw Dresden have been equipped, which will enable the public to send telegrams from on board these boats on end from the Ist July next. The other vessels on the Hook service are also being fitted with wireless telegraphy, and will be available to the publio shortly. WIRRAL AND BIRKENHEAD SHOW.

Mr. Brighouse opened an inquest at the Police Station on Tuesday night, touching the death of William Fletcher (aged OP Years who resided with his sister, Betay Ball, at 107, Bewsest-road) and who died in the Workhouse hospital on Sanday morning. —Mr. F. G. Taylor appeared for Messrs. Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iroe Comnony.—The Coroner said that for some years Fletcher had suffered f rom diabetes and shortly before Christmas he complained to his sister that be had burnt his toe with Some hot sand, whilst following bin employment as a labairer at the works of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company. HO continued hie work until February sth, when he went on the sick list. It was then found that be was suffering from gangrene on the toe. He was treated atilt() Infirm try, and was afterwards attended by Dr. Corker, who attributed death to diabetes, and considered the injury would not have cansed any ill effects if he had, not bean suffering from diabate3.— Dr. Hodgkinion stated that the itn-nediate canes of death was due to diabetic gangrene of .the toot. —The inquest was adjourned until Monday night. £ll 14s Good second-hand piano.—Wolo,London rd., Stockton Heath. Tunings and repairs.—Advt. Disastrous Farm Fire. A disastrous farm fire broke out shortly after three o'clock on Tuesday afternoon at Manor Heise Farm, Preston Brook, belonging-to Mr. Henry Whitlow. It started in a large new Dutch barn of six bays. con- taining about twenty tons of newly-gathered clover as well as a large quantity of straw, some machinery und vehicles, and is supposed to have been caused by the terrific heat of the sun. The Warring- . ton Fire Brigade was summoned by wire, and Deputy-Superintendent Turner and a number of men turned out with the Engine Major. In the meantime some fire appliances from the Dutton Union were got to work from a main, and they did useful service till the arrival of the brigade. The are was then burning fiercely and the flames had spread to the adjourning block of buildiags need as shippons and stables. A good supply of water was obtainable from a pit three hdndred yards away, and the mains. The roofs or both the barn and the shippon collapsed, ' and practically n ,thing remained of the former, while only the walls of the brick building were left stand-* ing. Among the debris were the remains of two lorries and two carts aid a ,number of badly damaged machines. The damage, which amounts to several hundred pounds, is covered by insurance. PUBLIC BENEFIT.--UNDER THE CLOCK iron. BICST BOOTS IN LANCISHIRE.—Acivt. „Suicide of an Ex-Sergeant's Wife. . The pathetic circumstances attending the death of Sarah Devlin; aged 58 years, of 22, Miller•street, Latchford, wife of Patrick Devlin, an ex•policesergeant formerly stationed at Sankey, were investigated at the Police 'Station. on Tuesday night by Mr. Coroner Brighoase and a jury.—The husband stated that for some time his wife had been suffering from cancer on the liver and had been under the care of Dr. Collins. She had been in bed except for a few hours since Thursday. She had suffered a great deal of pain. At abaut 10.45 on Sunday morning, witness took some soup upstairs to his wife and sat with her for a short time. He asked her if she was any better and she replied " about the same," and that she would get up when the house had been cleaned. Witness went downstairs at about 11.5, and shortly afterwards, in consequence of what his daughter Catherine said, and her screarns for help, he ran upstairs and found his wife with her throat eut, evidently by a razor. Dr. Robinson was called in, and he dressed the wound, but she died at 1.30. The Coroner, read a note which had been left by tha deceased saying "that she caild not stand the pain, and asked that the girls should be taken for a change and go into another house." Witness, continuing, said he had not the slightest suspicion that his wife would take away her life. The jury returned a verdict of "Suicide, whilst of unsound mind," and expressed their sympathy with the bereaved husband and family.

Next week about threehandred British photographers —amateur and profession d— vill 63 b icy in the ancient cities of Belgium, making negatives for many a series of lantern-slides to be used next winter for photographic and literary sooletiea' lactures. The Photographic Convention of the United King lam is Meeting in Brussels, its first visit bsyond the bone shores, and it is fortunate in making its first Continental experience in a country whore so much bomty and antiquity is ' compressed into so small a space. The Conventipuers are travelling by many rotates, but the largest play, I believe, is taking advantage of Beigiaa Sr,ate ttilway arrangements and the Dover-Ostende passage. div.head: TO ATTRACT ANI-31ALS.
div.p: TO ATTRACT ANI-31ALS.

A slight, peculiar, but not terrifying noise made by an assistant just at the right time will often secure the attention of an animal and keep it in good alert position for a number of seconds. Trundling a wheel-barrow, shaking a few marbles, very slowly revolving a " corn- crake" rattle, and making a slight hissing sound with the mouth, have all been used satisfactorily. Birds and animals may often be attracted to the position chosen by laying a train otismall portions of some favourite food.
INTERIOR AND EXTERIOR, AT ONE EXPOSURE.

Interiors of rooms incrudinr.' the view from the window can best be obtained by use of a flashlight exposure, so that the whole uncapping of the lens is not mare thin would be needed for the exterior view. Alternative methods are tb block the windows included in the picture by covering them with black cloth or paper outside, give the interior exposure with the light from other windows, cap the lens, remove the window-blocking, and expose for the landscape. Or, give the exposure for the landscape in the day-time, then cip the lens, leave the camera unmoved until night, and make the interior exposure by flashlight.

TO SAVE FOGGED PLATES. Plates which have been accidentally exposed to ligh t need not be thrown away. The silver can he removey from the gelatine entirory by fixing in the ordinary hypo bath, and then washing thoroughly. This leaves a flue gelatine film on the glass, which can be used for making stained light filters, or for transparencies by the ferro-prussiate and similar processes, or can be sensitised with bichromate and treated by development and staining, as in the Sanger-Shepherd three-colour method. Tha plates can also be made fit for e'xposure and development in the ordinary way by the following method :

Immerse for five minutes in chro:nio acid, ogr. ; potass bromide, 33gr.; water, 10z. Wash, dry. Reduces speed considerahly. They can also be made suitable for use as transparencies by soaking them in the following solution: —Potassium bromide, I oz. ; potassium iodide, GO gr. ; warm water, 2 oz. Worn dissolved add hydrochloric acid, 2 oz. ; potassium bichromite loz. ; water to 3oz. The plates should be well washed after inimersion(in the dark-room of course),snd dried. They will require eight times the normal exposure, and should be developed with hydroquinone.

div.p: A COUPLETE WORK-B00a;

The Photographic Annual, which is published to-day, bas been described as "mental pemmican," because it contains the boilei-down essence of such an enormous amount of practical matter. It deals with'every branch of photogriphy, from the work of the beginner to that of the most expert photographic and photo-mechanical worko s. It is divided into 38 sections, supplemented by a glossary and index which contains facts, de(lnitions, synonyms, cross references, etc. Wherever it gives instructions, they are cut down to the very fewest possible words, but it seems to me absolutely complete as a collection of formulre. Such diverse subjects as the painting of backgrounds, water-proofing and fire- proofing of fabrics, cleaning and cementing of lenses, exposure, development, light-filters, all the printing processes, optical lantern work and enlarging, photo- gravure, photo-engraving, colletype, iftc., have all their formula) given. Weights and measures, hygiene, copy- right, aids for tourists, and a host of other subjects era dealt with. The hook runs to 291 pages, and has a few , illustrations in the text, and its cost is only is., post free, is. 4d. from any dealer. I understand that the threo previous editions, which were only half the size of the present book,have gone out of print very rapidly and the publishers also inform me that as it is now to be issned es an annual, the matter in next year's volume will be verrlargely different, so that the pre- sent issue is likely to go oit of print quickly, and to appreciate in value. There is also a cloth-bound edition interleaved with writing paper for additional notes and memoranda, published at 2s.

div.head: LOOPING THE LOOP AT THE WHITE CITY.
div.p: LOOPING THE LOOP AT THE WHITE CITY.

"What won't people do and what risks won't some folk run in onier to gather in the shillings " was the caustic comment of an aged man to his wife the other evening in the White City, nanchester. Just ten seconds before the old couple had stood with mouths agape watching is nervy little cyclist dressed in white, madly propelling his cycle about a revolving globe. One slip meant serious injury and probably death for the plucky rider and a sigh of relief came from the audience milieu he had completed his sensational act. " Looping the loon " in a revolving globe DS performed by Mr. John Rohr, a member of the three riding Rohrs, a trio of the best known cyclists on the Continent is beyond a doubt one of the most sensational free shows offered. by the White City to its patrons this season. For five long years Rohr (who in his day was considered Germany's ,fastest sprint rider) has been at work on the revolving globe, incidentally figuring out how to defy gravitation. That he has at last succeeded is best, judged by. the thunderons applause which daily greets the conclusion of his performance in the White City. But the nervy rider bears on various parts of his body route evidence of how he has courted with death during the past three years. His collar bone has twice been broken, one leg, and then an arm. But still the performer would not give in. " I can defy gravitation and give the public an act differ- ent from any they have seen " was his reply to the Urgings of friends. In most other looping the loop inventions, the rider is helped by mechanical cottriv- maces, such as a motor cycle, invisible wire attached to the body in case of an accident, &c. Rohr however must depend upon his sturdy leg power and guiding ability. With his two partners mounted on cycles he tears madly about the interior of the steelllobe. In addition he pick § up a handkerchief from the floor of the cage while riding about its perpendicular sides at terrific speed, and then startles his• audience by riding through a hoop at top speed. It was with diffi- culty that Mr. J. Calvin Brown, managing director of the White City induced the Three Rohrs to come to Manchester, as they are contracted for two years in America. They finally agreed, hoe ever, to come simply as a compliment to two Manchester engineers, who aided thorn in putting together their most remarkable globe of death.—With the summer season now on in earnest thousands are flocking to Manchester's White City to enjoy its myriads of amusements, and bear the excellent concerts of the White City Military Band, tinder the leadership of Mr. W. Wallbank, one of the best known musicians in Northern England.

HE HAD NO CHEST. Pat Murphy had been out of work for some time, and was a few weeks in arrears with his rent, so he determined to enlist, consoling him- self with the thought that the life of a soldier would not be worse than being in lodgings. All went well till Pat was in the ranks for drill, and the sergeant called out, "Here, Murphy, throw out your chest." "Sorry, sir, I can't," replied Pat. "Can't! Why ?" " Because my landlady has it, sir." SHIRTS. Two Irishmen bought some shirts. When they got home, one of them found out that his shirt was too small. He shouted to Pat, " This shirt is too small; What shall I do? " " Oh," replied the other, "cut a piece off the top and stitch it on the bottom."

INLAND O R RES PO-NDENC

The term ‘7l;iTa:nd Correspondence " means cor- respondence posted within the United Kingdom, including the Isle of Man and the Channel islands. "Inland Correspondence" is divided into the following classes : (a) Letters (d) Newspapers (b) Postcards (e) Parcels (c) Halfpenny packets Not only letters, but any document or article (with a few trifling exceptions) which can be trans- mitted by post at all, may be sent by letter post, the only limitation being that of size. LETTER POST. The prepaid rate of postage is its follows : Not exceeding 4 ozs. in weight ... Id. For every additional 2 0z5.... A letter posted unpaid is chargeable on delivery with clouble postage; a letter insuMcieutly paid, with double the deficiency. No letter may exceed two feet in length, one foot in width, or one foot in depth. • POST-CARDS. The prepaid rate of postage on every post-card is one half-penny, and on every reply post-card one penny. A post-card poited unpaid is chargeable on delivery with one penny. Cards used as post-cards must be made of ordinary card-board, not thicker than the material used for f the thickest official post-card. They may not exceed 53 inches in length by 3i inches in width, or be less then 31 inches in length by 21 inches in width. A gummed label (not to exceed 2 inches long and :2-inch wide) bearing the address may now be atlixed to the address side of card. If any of the rules relating to a post-card be infringed, the curd will ho treated as a letter. HALrPENVY PACKET POST. The Halfpenny Packet Post can be used only for packets not exceeding 2oz. in weight. Printed matter, &c., rirtt in the nature of a letter, • may bo transmitted by this method. NEWSPAPER POST., The prepaid rate of postage on a registered news- paper, including any supplement thereto, whether posted singly or with others is J. Newspspers not registered at the General Post Olice are treated in the pcst like any other printed matter. _

PARCEL POST. The rates of postage on parcels areas follows: For a parcel not exceeding 1 lb. 0 3 f exceeding 1 lb. If 2 lb. 0 4 2 lb. If 3 lb. 0 5 ft „ 3 lb. 5 lb. 0 0 „ 5 lb. 7 lb. 0 7 ~ 7 lb. 8 lb. 0 8 ft „ 8 lb. If 9 lb. 0 9 If ft 9 lb. 10 lb. 010 10 lb. „ 11 lb. 0 11 No parcel may exceed 11 lb. in weight. The size allowed for an inland parcel is : Greatestlength... ... 3 ft. 6 in. Greatest length and girth combined 6 ft. 0 in. For example—A parcel measuring 3ft. Gin, in its longest dimensions as much as 2ft. Gin. round its thiekest part ; a short parcel may be thioker ; thus, if it measnre no more than 3ft. in length, it may measure as much as aft. round its thickest part. The postage on a parcel must be prepaid. Mark each parcel Parcel Post." A parcel must not be posted in a letter box, but presented at the oounter of a post office, and the sender should see that the weight, size and postage are in order before leaving. PARCELS (ForteleN AND COLONIAL). Parcels are accepted for parcel post to most foreign countries under conditions similar to the inland regulations, except that for customs require- ments the contents must be declared. The eastorris charges can be prepaid or collected bn delivery. The postage varies to different countries and must be prepaid. MONEY' ORDERS (INLAND.) . The postal authorities cannot issue a single money order for mor3 than £4O, and will only cash them at the money order office at which they are made payable, unless they are crossed, when they can be paid through a bank. No fractional part of a id. eau be contnined in a money order. The rates of poundage are :—Not exceeding £l, 21. ; £3, 3d.; £lO, 41.; £2O, 6J. ; £3, Bd. ; £4), 10d. By paying an additional 2d. and cost of the telegram of advice, a money order can be 'telegraphed under certain restrictions. MONEY ORDF.RS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL.) The maximum amount for which a money order i may be issued for places abroad varies n each particular place. The poundage rates are :—Not oxceedine£l,Si.; £2, 6d. ; and above that, 3d. for each additional £2 or portion of it. A fee of 6cl. in addition to the ordinary poundage, together with cost of telegram of advice, enables money orders to be telegraphed to certain places abroad. POSTAL ORDERS. These are obtainable at any money order office in the United Kingdom, and possess the advantage over money orders that they can be cashed at any money order office. If crossed, they can be paid into a bank. They are issued for fixed amounts, rising by 6d., from 6d. to £1 Is. The poundage fees are :—.lcl. up to 2s. 61.; Id. up to 1.55.; I Ad. up to 21s. Before parting with a postal order, always fill in the name of the person to whom the amount is to be paid. Each order is numbered, as Is also the counterfoil attached, which latter should be retained and name of payee tilled in. The Post- master-General will entertain no further claim after an order is once paid. Stamps to the amount of sd. can be affixed to make up odd sums. TELEGRAMS (INLAND). The Postmaster-General possesses,almost entirely, the privilege of transmitting,colleeting and deliver- ing telegrams in the United Kingdom. The charge for a telegram is a minimum amount of 6d., which covers 12 words, and an additional Ad. for each extra word. This charge includes delivery within the postal district if sent out for delivery from a head telegraph office, but if from a sub-office then within three miles only, beyond which a charge of fid. per mile is made from the office door. All charges are, as far as possible, prepared by affixing stamps to telegrrm form. Address of person receiv- ing a telegram has to be paid far, but sender's name if written on back of form need not be. Five figures count as one word. The cost of a reply may be prepaid. Telegrams can be repeated on payment of half the original charge, which extra payment is refunded if error is detected. Telegrams may be posted in wall or pillar boxes, or handed to rural postmen, and are wired as soon as received at the nearest telegraph office. Late fees secure attention, in certniu caseg, to telegrams handed in after the usual hours. The cost of registering an abbrevi- ated address, which must consist of two words, is £1 Is.

—.-- TELEGRAMS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL) Must be written on special forms and are accepted in the language of any of the principal European countries. The rates vary, and are too numerous to detail here,

div.head: POST OFFICE SAVINGS BANK.
div.p: POST OFFICE SAVINGS BANK.

These are established at all money order offices. In ordinary cases the annual deposit must not exceed £5O, and the total amount £2OO. No person can have more than one account. Amounts placed in the bank on behalf of children under seven years of age cannot be withdrawn until the child reaches that age, and then only under his or her own signa- ture. The smallest amount received at a time is Is., and this may take the form of 12 penny stamps affixed to R special form. Each depositor receives a bank book in which the amount of each deposit should he entered at the time of paying in. If the deposit is el or over; a spacial acknowledgment is sent from the head London office. Interest is allowed at the rate of 21 per cent. Any amount up to and including .2t m,ty ho withdrawn withont previous notice, on presenting n bank book. 'rho bank book should be sent each year, postage free, on the anniversary of the date when the account was opened, to the Controller of the Savings Bank Department for purposes of checking and adding interest. The withdrawal ot money can be expedited by telegraphing, the depositor paying cost of telegrams. _ _

div.head: MOTOR CAR AND CYCLE REr4ULATIONS.
div.p: MOTOR CAR AND CYCLE REr4ULATIONS.

Each one must be registered with the council of n county or county borough, the fee being £1 for a motor car, and ss. for a motor cycle. A registered number is assigned to each, which it is an offence not to keep affixed when driving. Each driver must possess a license, costing 55., to be renewed every 12 months, and obtainable from the county authorities, which may be endorsed or suspended for reckless driving or certain other offences. The highest speed at which a car msy be driven on the public highways is 20 miles an hour, which is reduced to 10 miles under special local regula- tions.
It is an offence under the Motor Car Act (1003), to drive a car in such a way on a public highway as to be dargerouS to the public, having regard to all the circumstances of the case. -

....... „. In the event of an accident to any person due to On presence of the motor car on the rend, the driver must supply his name and address, and the owner and number of the car, under heavy penal- ties. The driver must produce his licence at the request of a police constable.
The Examiner, Saturday July 4, 1908.

div.head: Atheism at Bridge Foot.
div.p: Atheism at Bridge Foot.

Sir,—May I be permitted to say a word on an ' atheistical lecture, delivered near the Iron Bridge, last Thursday evening. There was an eager crowd, who, from personal observations, entirely appeared to agree with the speaker. Ills subject, from enquiries made was : " Jesus Christ a blind guide." His attack was generally directed to the four Canonical Gospels. Now I ara-Pot prepare4,to say whether it is right or wrong for this kind of propaganda to be allowed or not. But Ido honestly and sincerely think, that our local and professional preachers should attack it, and thus prove (if possible), slbether the people are being deluded, or not. There were a few questions put to the speaker, at the close of the meeting, which he apparently had no dia:culty in answering. Now I suggest that this should be left to able and competent persons, especially those who are being paid to preach and defend our religion. This lecturer stated his intention of again visiting Warrington on Thursday, July 9th, and that he i was prepared to meet any theologian n debate: Then I trust that some reverend gentleman will cometforward and settle his hash, and so prevent any more atheistica discussion and distribution of blasphemous pamphlets. J.W.B. June 29th, 1903.

Holidays for Poor and Crippled Children Dear Sir,—May we plead with your readers once again for liberal help with our Holiday Homes Fond? It is scarcely realised what it means to many of these poor and crippled children to have a chance of getting a good healthy grip on life, which comes from a fort- night's stay in the country under wholesome influences and surroundings. Many of them are weakly and would soon go under altogether but for the opportunities thus ! afforded of rest and change. Such a necessary holiday is worth a very great deal to these children who are ! mainly identifled with our 110 affiliated Mission Centres In the poorest parts of London, in addition to a large number selected from our register of over seven thousand crippled children. On behalf of these handi- capped little ones tho Council would again ask for financial assistance, earnestly trusting the aid will , be as generous as possible to onable them to carry onl this most necessary and rertinceratir work for another ' season. It may be added that the parents are expected to a.ssist in the cost whenever possible, and care is taken to prevent overlapping. Not nntrequently how- ever, help has to be rendered with clothing and boots, . thereby increasing the expense. For thousands of these poor children, as well as for some of the old folks, there must alas ! still be only the " Day in the Country." For this shorter spell of happiness, the Council likewise earnestly plead.—Yours faithfully, JOHN KIRK, Director. Ragged School Union and Shafteshury Society (Ostablished 1841). 32, John at., Theobald's rd., London, W.C.

div.head: Mr. Howes and the Labour Party.
div.p: Mr. Howes and the Labour Party.

Sir,—A well-known Liberal protagonist answering a question, at a meeting last week, held under the auspices of the Progressive Labour League denied the representatives in the House of Commons that recognise the leadership of Mr. A. Henderson are a Labour party. Quite on the contrary : " Every man who is connected with Labour is a member of the Labour party and it is the greatest piece of impudent arrogance for a handful of Socialists to call themselves the Labour party." The " Daily Chronicle (Liberal) Parliamentary guide' writes as follows of these "handful of Socialists." "In this election (MS) a new element appeared in strength in the shape of fifty-one candidates supported and financed by the Labour Representation Committee in conjunction with the trade unions. It was the Taff Vale decision which made Labour representation on the present scale possible. The great trade unions are wealthy and powerful organisations. Finding, as they believed, the very principle of their existence menaced they resolved to seek redress by means of direct representation in Parliament. The Labour Representa- tion Committee was formed by resolution of the Trade Union Congress. The co-oporatien of the Independent Labour Party and of the Fabian Society, two Socialist organisations, both of which had made the cause of Labour their own, was welcomed, and these two bodies were affiliated to the Labour Representation Com- mittee. By means of a small annual levy upon a million trade unionists the Labour Representation Comrsittee was able not only to pay the election expenses of its candidates but also to form a fund out of which could be paid ,C2OO per annum for the maintenance of each elected Member of Parliament. At the time of the election this Labour Representation Committee Labour party had formulated no official programme. Its first and all-absorbing object is to be —to exist—in independence of all parties. Among its candidates were comprised persons who had been acti re Liberal workers in the past and active Socialists, and at least one Unionist. But the Labour Representa- tion Committee itself is not Socialist any more than it is Liberal or Conserratire. It is essentially trade union and the one test is that its candidates must be prepared to do everything in their power in Parliament to strengthen the power and protect the rights of organised labour and to act together independently of other parties." The list of occupations of the "middle class Socialist party " does not present such a glorious array of dukes and mining magnates. I think you will find more of that ilk amongst the orthodox political parties. Answer- ing questions re the Unemployed Workmen Bill at the same meeting Mr. Howes said "The Labour party never introduced the Bill. The Socialists did, but the Labour party did not." If my memory serves me right I believe it was that young Liberal Member for ; South St. Pancras (Mr. Philip W. Wilson) that intro- duced the Bill,and I find in the division list 74 Liberals —supporters of the Government that had the courage to defy the crack cf the party Whip and vote for this "silly" Bill. Amongst the 71 that had the arrogance to "play at fooling at legislation " were stalwarts like C. F. G. Masterman (a member of the Ministry), W. Abram (Mabon), Percy Alden, Hilaire Belloc, R. Cameron, Sir It. Cramer, E. Edwards (Chairman of the Liberal Labour Group), Charlie Fenwick, Carrie Grant, R. C. Lehmann, L. G. C. Money, E. H. Pickersgill, J. Havelock Wilson, &c. There is a possibility of some of the above-mentioned M.P.'s appearing here in the near future and a free copy of the " Examiner " containing a report of the Ellesmere-street meeting or a concise question with regard to their " play at fool- ing at legislation " vote might have an interesting result. At any rate I feel it will be rather a difficult job for some of our politicians who will have the onerous task placed on their shoulders of defending the representative that abstaired from voting, the repre- sentative that voted for the Bill, and the representative that voted against the "accurs't thing."—Yours &c. G PsS WO R

The picturesquely situated Parish Church at Lymm was the scene of a wedding in which great interest was taken on 'Thursday, when the Rev. David Richard Davies, of All Hallows Church, Kendal, son of the 4te Mr. Richard Davies, of Cardiff, was married to Miss Anita Mary Totlhunter, daughter of the late Mr J. M. if. Todhunter, of Lynam. The bride• groom was formerly curate at St. James's, Latchford, and before going to Kendal he was at Lymm Parish Church. The esteem in which both bride and bridegroom are held in the district was evidenced by the large congregation which assembled to witness the ceremony. The church was very beautifully decor- ated with florrers. Tho cfficiating clergy were the Rev. W. J. Davies, Vicar of St. Asaph, (brother of the bridegroom), and the Rev. G. B. Thurston, rector of Lymm. The service was choral, Mr. Cook presiding . at the organ. The hymns "0 God, our help in ages past " and " 0 perfect Love" were sung and at the dose of the service the organist played Mendelssohn's Wedding March. The bride, who was given away by her uncle,. Mr. W. Milner, of Warrington, was -charmingly attired in white crilpe-de•cbene over white silk, trimmed with silver and white lace, with silver belt and slippers. She carried a bouquet of white roses, stephanotis and lilies of the valley, and wore a gold chain with pearl and ruby pendant, the gift of the bridegroom. There were no bridesmaids. Mr. T. E. Davies, of Afrilvern (brother of the bridegroom) discharged the duties of best man. After the cere- mony a reception was held by Miss Milner, the aunt of the bride, at The Limes, Lymm, a large number of guests attending. Later in the day the happy couple left for their honeymoon tour, the bride's travelling dress being a white serge costume, with pale pink crepe-cle-ehene blouse, trimmed with lace. She wore a white lade hat, trimmed with pink westeria and pink rose. Numerous handsome presents were received.

div.head: MR. A. H. GROSFIELD, M.P. AND CURRENT POLITICS.
div.p: MR. A. H. GROSFIELD, M.P. AND CURRENT POLITICS.
THE OLD-AGE PENSIONS SCHEME.

The following letter from Mr. Crosfield M.P. to Mr. Morton (secretary of the Progressive Labour League) only reached us last Friday night, too late for insertion in last week's paper. We are sure it will interest cur readers, expressing as it does, the Member's views on current politics. II)de Park Gate, London, June 23th, 1995.

Dear Mr. Morton, The Progressive Labour League are having a busy time of it in Warrington this week; and that prompts me to write you briefly —very briefly —on a few of the greater issues we have been dealing with in the House here. _ _ _

The Licensing Bill will be chiefly considered in the Autumn Session, but I expect we may get through the first clause or two of it before we break up for the holidays. We are determined to make this Bill a success, and I think it is pretty evident that its main features already command in the country, not only assent, but very hearty thorough-going, determined support. When the Bill was introduced one heard some gloomy prophecies as to its effect on the Liberal I Party. Do we hear one of them now ? How many people now have the hardihood to attack the principle of a reasonable tirne ? The numbers of uncom• promising opponents of this measure have grown gradually small and beautifully less, and few there are nowadays who offer any real and genuine opposi- tion to the closing of redundant public-houses, many of them run at little or no profit. On this, the greatest political controversy of the present time, opinion in the country has ripened, and ripened very fast too. It has ripened on another subject, also one of paramount national importance, and I think that any political leader, however eminent, will find that he is playing with fire if he uses his influence and position in order to frustrate the concordat on the Education question which everyone is locking for. At the moment we are in the thick of the problems —and deeply important problems they are too - involved in the question of old age pensions. As you and I are well aware, by iutroducing and carrying tins immensely important measure, we are fulfilling pledges given by our political opponents. They made the promises : we fulfil them. Seven millions sterling per annum is more than any State, however high its tariffs, has yet granted to the aged poor, and that amidst plenty of criticism, is the first essential fact to be borne in mind. We have been asked to make our scheme contribu- tory, but this would have excluded from it women, and all that class of labour which is employed irregu- lady and at a specially low wage. Well these are the very people in the community whom we want to save if we can in old age from the Poor House. Two important changes we have made in the Bill this week, and I voted for both of them ; the reduction for two people of one family living in the same house has been cancelled to the satisfaction of the great majority of the House, and I am glad to say we have adopted the sliding scale instead of a bard and fast 103. limit. If you consider the two al ternatives,i have little doubt that you will think as I do that there is a good deal to be said on both sides, but to my mind the balance is strongly in favour of the sliding scale, even though it be a scale from 83. to 13s. I would like to see a graduated scale from 10s. to 155., and my intention is at present to vote in favour of that alteration. But I must make this proviso : I would not dream of giving a single vote that would be likely to jeopardise the fate of a Bill which, incomplete as it is, is of euch importance to the country. So even on this question of a 10s. to 15s. limit, I shall net finally make up my mind till one sees how things stand in the House at the time, and probably I shall discuss that important issue with my friend Maddison. lam truly glad lie is coming to address your Leave to-morrow, and I don't know anyone in the House who more honestly and thoroughly unites a courageous, generous, large- hearted view of measure: for the public good, with that prudence and level-he,aded experience, which in these days are an invaluable combination in politics. I am sure he will have an appreciative and keenly interested audience when he addresses the members of your League to-morrow night, and I hope that not- notwithstanding the manifold attractions of a summer's evening in June you will have an excellent and very useful meeting: I for one can never forget the most powerful and indeed valuable part played by the League in the great victory we won at the last elec- tion, and I do not doubt the good cause of well ordered progress will have its equally powerful back- ing in the future. With kindest remembrances and good wishes to all members of the League, believe me, dear Mr. Morton, Very faithfully yours, A. 11. CROSFIELD.

Magistrate and Music Licences. At the Warrington Borough Court, on Thursday, several publicans were granted music: licences on the occasion of Walking Day. Mr. W. Roberts (a magistrate) said that Walking Day was a Sunday school festival, and why they should grent special facilities to publicans at a time like that he could not understand. It seethed to him a funny way of keeping up a Sunday school festival. Although he would not oppose the applications that time he wished it to be known that he strongly objected to them. He would rather the publicans did not apply at that time, as it seemed to him a fume.

div.head: WALKING DAY, YESTERDAY'S SUCCESSFUL
div.p: WALKING DAY, YESTERDAY'S SUCCESSFUL
FESTIVAL.
ROMAN CATHOLIC PROCESSION.
Brilliant Display.

There was only one opinion of yesterday's Roman Catholic procession. It was the best ever seen in the town. The members of this Church always excel in the beauty of their pageantry. That love of the ornate and beautiful which is so striking a feature of their religious system always finds ex p cession on this occasion, and there can be few more charming spectacles than Warrington's Roman Catholic pageant. Yesterday's display, too, showed what a great advantage it is to have such a wide thoroughfare as Bridge-street now is. The promoters of the procession were able to carry out an entirely new arrangement which considerably ...enhanced the dignity of the general effect. Our Lady's school, Latchford, was the first to make its appearance. Passing over Warrington Bridge it traversed Bridge-street to Market-gate then turned round and retraced its way along the other side of the thoroughfare. It was immediately followed by the other Roman Catholic schools which went as far as Bridge-foot and then returned to Market-gate. The result was a brilliant scene the like of which has never before been . witnessed in Bridge-street. While some schools were wending their way along one side of the street, more were passing in the opposite direction on the other side There was a perfect forest of magnificent banners while exquisite floral devices were also held aloft. Here and there one saw a glittering processional cross followed , by acolytes. The costuming and grouping of the chil- dren were perfect. Each school followed out some distinctive scheme. Many of the scholars carried wands tipped with flowers and wore sashes of various delicate tints. The little girls had garlands on their heads and savral figured as May Queens and walked with an air of dignity, attended by their train bearers. One contingent of boys and girls looked exceedingly well as Italian gypsies, with turbans, gay ribbons and jingling tambourines. The banners were many and beautiful. One set was illustrative of the seven Sacraments whilst others depicted , the Virgin and great Saints of the Church. There were many beautiful statues of the Virgin, embowered in lilies and greenery, and floral harps and crosses, an effective representation of the rosary, and other features too numerous to mention made up a picture which was so impressive as frequently to call forth the applause of the onlookers. The Mayor and Mayoress and Mr. and Mrs. A. H. Crosfleld witnessed the pageant from the upper windows of Atkinson's Cafe'. One thing contributed much to the success of the display—the public were induced to keep to the footpaths and allow the processionists ample room instead of crowding into the middle of the road as has too often been the case. A special word of praise is duo to the Chief Constable (Mr. M. Nicholls) for the excellent police arrangements. He and his officers worked hard and kept the great crowds in hand, with the result that everything passed off without a single untoward incident.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

LIBERAL CLUB.—The bowling picnic, which was pro- posed at the lest general meeting, took place on Saturday afternoon in glorious weather, the place chosen being Frodsham. The members, numbering 23, left Penketh in a four-in-hand bus at 1.30 p.m., reaching the Red Lion Hotel, Frodsham, at four o'clock. Games were at once indulged in,the chief event being a bowling main. The entrants included all members present, and many interesting and exciting finishes resulted. The prize-winnors were :-1, Harry Bowyer ; 2, S. Tunstall ;3, Fred Dale ; 4, Bruno Hoyser. Tea was partaken of, after which the President (Mr. Richard Routledge) congratulated the members on the success of the inaugural picnic. Tea over, some of the members took advantage of the picturesque surroundings and visited the hills. The party left Frodsham at nine o'clock, after having spent an enjoyable afternoon. Mr. 11. Davies (hon. secretary) and the committee are to be congratulated on their excellent arrangements.

FitrENDLY* SOCIFITY NEWFS.—On Friday last the Penketh United Order of Druids held their quarterly lodge night. 13ro. J. Leigh, N.S., presided, and was assisted by Bro. W. Tarburton, 47.0. A. This Lodge is a most thriving one. No Lodge night comes round without several new members being initiated.—There were two on Friday night Bro. David Houghton, P.G.M., in a few choice remarks of welcome to the new mem- bers said that being members of a friendly Society I would qualify them for the Government old-age pensions. Daring the evening Bro. John Leigh, N.G.A., and Bro. J. J. Worsley were presented with an illumin- ated emblem of the Order for their services. Bro. David Houghton performed the presentation in well chosen words and wished the recipients success. (Applause.) Bros. Leigh and Worsley thanked the Lodge for the emblems and assured the Brothren that anything they could do for the welfare of the Order they would cheerfully do. Bro. Woods also added his testimony to the efforts put forward by the Brothers. Bro. A. T. May proposed a vote of thanks to P.G.M. Houghton, which was seconded by Bro. Aldcroft and carried. This brought the evening to a close.

div.head: DEATH OF MRS. ELLEN' BOOTH.
div.p: DEATH OF MRS. ELLEN' BOOTH.
Stockton Heath's Oldest Inhabitant.

Stockton Heath has lost one of its oldest and best- known inhabitants by the death of Mrs. Ellen Booth, who passed away suddenly on Tuesday morning. Mrs. Booth was born in 1819 and had spent her entire life in the village. She was for many years a trusted servant of the late Mr Robert Davies and .continued to give help to his household until his death. .

Religiously her experience was an interesting one. She attended the Barn Sunday School and learned to read, as did many other village children, under the care of Peter and Joshua Phillips, who used the barn door as their blackboard as they taught the mysteries of music and spelling. When the building of a chapel was projected she collected pennies to buy bricks for it and to the end of life remembered with keen interest her early efforts for the cause. The chapel was duly built in 1827, and now does service as the Independent Methodist Sunday sohool. She remembered most of the famous men who used to visit the barn and chapel and was among those who joined the first total abstinence society formed in 1831 She maintained to the last an active sympathy with the Church and was present last Sunday morning at the service. Monday was spent in visiting relatives and it is surmised that she contracted a heat stroke, for on Tuesday morning after a seizure lasting only a few minutes he passed away. The funeral took place on Thursday at Hill Cliff e graveyard, Mr. A. Mounfleld conducting the service.

div.head: BATHING FATALITY AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: BATHING FATALITY AT WARRINGTON.
Would-be Rescuer's Narrow Escape.

A sad bathing fatality occurred on Wednesday after- noon in the river just beyond Manor Lock, Warrington. Robert M`Millan, 35 years of age, 4, Brook-place. Latchford, went with a friend named Crutchley to bathe. The latter entered the water first, and M`Millan followed, but had only gone a few yards when he threw up his arms. Crutchley went to his assistance, and turned him towards the bank' when he seemed to be all right. Both men then struck out for the bank, when M‘Millan seized hold of Crutchley's ankle. They went under, and Crutchley managed to get clear, when a lock-keeper named Shaw threw a rope to him and he was pulled to the bank. ArMillan immediately sank, and his body was later recovered.

div.head: MR. MADDISON AND HIS SEAT.
div.p: MR. MADDISON AND HIS SEAT.

Mr. F. Maddison, M.P., has addressed the following letter to the 4ditor of the" Manchester Courier." Sir,—l have just seen the following quotation from an account of a Tory meeting at Burnley, which appeared in your paper: "It has lately become known that the present Labour member for Burnley, Mr. Maddison, is not eager—in some quarters it is said that he is even unwilling—to again contest the' Division." I should be glad to know what is the source of your Information. It certainly did not come from me, and I am not aware of anything in the situation at Burnley to make me less eager to fight, than I was at the last election. As for the statement that lam not willing to stand again, I have only one trifling objection to it —it is not true. Of course the question of the next election has not been discussed between the Liberal leaders at Burnley and myself, but you may rest assured when the time comes for the fight, the Liberalism of the borough will give a good account of itself. F. MADDISON. 12, Acne-street, Wandsworth, London, S.W. June 2Uth

Mach talk has been caused in the lobby by the statement that Lord Derby has resigned his position as vice-chairman of the Lancashire County Association of the Perritoriai Army. His action (says the London correspondent of the Liverpool Post and Mercury ") is justly or unjustly ascribed to disappointment at his not receiving the Lord-Lieutenancy of Lancashire. The House of Stanley seems to consider that they have almost a hereditary claim t 3 this great position, and the greatest pressure was brought to bear with the view of securing the office for the present Earl of Derby. That the noble lord should exhibit any annoy- ance or irritation at this matter must be a matter of sincere regret to his friends both in and out of Parlia- ment. He has taken an interest in the Territorial Army scheme, and has laboured to secure its success, but he is greatly mistaken if he thinks that his withdrawal from the County Association will mAterially affect the progress of the scheme. Whether the retirement of Captain Molynenx from the office of vice-chairman of the West Lancashire Branch has any connection with the appointment to the Lord-Lieutenancy is not known, but it is suspected that he is inspired by the same reasons as Lord Derby.

'Fatal Fall Downstairs. Thomas Meshock, 231, Winwick-road, died in the Infirmary yesterday morning as the result of a fall downstairs. On Thursday night he went upstairs to attend to a child who was crying and he was coaling down again when he slipped and fell to the bottom, fracturing his skull. Funeral of a Warrington Volunteer. The funeral ,took place at the Warrington Cemetery on Thursday of Sergeant Max leixdorf, of Napier- street, who for about ten years had been a member of the local Volunteer battalion, and served in South Africa with Major Appleton's company. The Revs. Canon Willis and W. Bracecamp officiated, and a number of deceased's comrades in the battalion acted as bearers. Major Appleton and Lieutenant Fairclough were present Station Thief Sentenced. At Manchester Assizes, on Wednesday, was heard the last of the sensational railway robbery, discovered at the Central Station, Warrington, when Margaret Gardiner, was sentenced to twelve months hard labour The police did not believe that prisoner had any accomplices. Prisoner, who had previously pleaded I guilty, never looked up as the judge addressed her. " Despite your grief," he said, "I am satisfied you are a very bad character, and one of those railway trtvelling thieves. You must go to prison Lr twelve months, with hard labour." Motor Speed Prosecutions. At Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednes- day morning, Alfred Au-tin Baxter, Preston Brook, was summoned for driving a motor-car at Newton:in- , Makerfield at a speed exceeding twenty miles an hour ' on May 22.—Mr.-Arthur Smith, of Wigan, stated that police were stationed on a two m:le measured distance at Winwick. On the date in question Ilaydock races were taking place, and there was a considerable amount of traffic on the road. Defendant drove his rear at such a speed as to exceed the limit.—The magistrates imposed a fine of £1 and costs.—Frank Pearce, Wilpshire, Blackburn, was fined id. and costs, for having exceeded the speed limit at Wiawick, on May 23. The police stated that defendant was driving at the rate of 30 miles an hour. New Footbridge at Howley. At a meeting of the General Purposes Committee hold at the Town Hall on Monday, under the presi- dency of the Mayor, a scheme for the ereation ef a footbridge across the Mersey at Howley, with a view to opening up Victoria: Park and providing better communication between Howley and Latchford, was unanimously approved, the cost not to exceed C. 603. When put in hand the work will only tike six weeks to complete. It will be an iron suspension bridge similar to the one crossing the Dee at Chester near the boat houses, but not on quite such an elaborate scale. The distance by road from the Parish Church to Black Bear Bridge —along Church-street, Mersey- street and Knutsford-road —is a mile and a quarter, and that fact in itself will show what a great saving of time and labour will be effected by the erection of the proposed bridge. Some little time will elapse before the work is begun, as tenders will have to be invited after the Council has passed tha scheme next Tuesday.

ANOTHER BETTING CASE. A Fine of £lO And Costs. At the Borough Police Court on Monday, before the Mayor (Alderman Smethurst) and a full Bench of magistrates, Frank Page, 44, Mill-lane, was summoned for frequenting Quay-fold for the purpose of betting on June 9th. Mr. J. W. Knowles, solicitor, represented the defendant and pleaded not guilty. The evidence of the police was to the effect that on June 9th, Dectectives Woollacott and Holland secreted themselves in the neighbourhood of Quay-fold, and saw defendant receive slips of paper, which appeared to contain money, from eight different men. The defend- ant's brother then came on the scene, and he handed to him the slips and the money, and recorded the transac- tions in a pocket book. When searched at the police station no slips, and only one halfpenny in money were found in defendant's possession. Mr. Knowles :—Do they take halfpenny bets in Warrington? (Laughter). Detective Woollacott : I don't think so. Mr. Knowles questioned both witnesses closely as to whether they actually saw money pass, and the Chief Constable said as it was quite immaterial whether there was money or not he would allow Mr. Knowles to take it that there was none. Mr. Knowles addressed the Bench on a point of law, and contended that defendant onght to have been sum- moned for loitering, because it had been held by learned judges that there must be more than one occasion to constitute frequenting. Therefore be hoped the Bench would not convict and put his client to the expense of aoing to the High Court to have it quashed. The magistrates having considered the case in private, the Mayor said defendant would be tined £lO and casts.

NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Cricket. W-arrington have had an inglorious season so far, and on Saturday they once mPro tasted the bitterness of defeat. The match was a League engagement with Present, and the Warringtonians were beaten on their own ground by a majority of 33. The Presoet men had first innings and although they started unpromisingly, they soon recovered themselves and rau up a total of 123. The most successful batsmen were J.M. Swift and D. Prescott, who made 39 and 31 respectively. Warrington made a good start but the visitors always played a winning game, their fielding being particularly smart. The innings realized 81, W. H. Podmore being the top contributor with a faultless 27. J. Callon was also in good form and knocked up 21, whilst W. Richardson was responsible for 16. . Warrington 2nd are doing far better than their sensiors. They have not been beaten once this season, and Saturday saw them in better form than ever, Prescot 2nd being easily accounted for. Batting first, Present, with the exception of S. Davies, failed against the deliveries of Bennett, who has the remarkable record of not having been compelled te relinquish bowling in any single game this season. On Saturday, he bowled with deadly effect, securing eight wickets at a coat of 35 runs. Warrington made light of their task. and after P. B. Havvtin (25) and A. The wlis (33) had given the side a good send-off, useful contributions brought up the aggregate to 274 for the loss of nine wickets. Well dona,Wartington 2nd ! St. James's continue their victorious career in the Warrington and District League. Oa Saturday they met Rylands's and defeated them by 40 runs. Holt distinguished himself with a flue batting display which realized 21. -- There was a keen encounter between the "Guardian" Office and Walker's brewery, victory resting with the brewery by the narrow margin of three runs. Rylands did good service for the victors, his contribution being 27, while Mines and Clarke batted well for the losers, with 16 runs each. In the Warrington and District Junior League St. James's severely trounced St. Mary's, the majority being 69. H. Ditchfleld and J. Warburton batted splendidly, each making 25. ----- Warrington Excelelors beat All Saints by 3 runs, thanks largely to the splendid bowling of Caldwell who took 8 wickets for 27 runs. H. Wilcock (16) was the top scorer for Exceigors, G. Monks making 19 not out for the losers. Sankey defeated Marshhonse-lane, their most success- ful batsman being S. Oregson (10). Whitfield took five wickets for seven runs. -- Warrington Grammar School 21i were lucky in beating Penketh Friends' School, the majority being two. Not a single player reached double figures. -- Warrington Commercials entertained the Birkenhead knights of the road and suffered a severe drabbing, the adverse margin being not far short of 109. Massey (44) was in great form for the winners, while F. Barber (16) and W. P. Ashton (13) geve the best display for Warrington. -- Latchford Baptists scored a triumph at tho expense of Rusholme, the margin being 36. Cliffa and J. Shanks batted well for their respective sides, making 52 and 37 respectively. A. Warhurst also bowled effectively for the home team taking six wickets for 20 runs. --- Orford had no difficulty in beating T. Allen and Sons, S. Leigh taking six wickets for 11 runs. Orford reserves met the Secondary School and were defeated by six runs. Parsonage captured seven wickets for five runs. -- Grappenhall first failed against Knotty Ash who won by 6 runs. E. Wilkinson (24 not oat) was the highest scorer for the vinners, while J. Warburton batted well for his 23 for Grappenhall. -- Grappenhall 2nd fared worse against Knotty Ash 2nd who ran up a majority of 30. S. Farmer (15) headed the scores for the winners, while " Mr. Extras " with .10 was Grappenhall's chief contributor. -- Moore and Daresbury entertained Barnton and were beaten by 32. A. Ellis (18) and J. Burgess (16) were the top scorers for Barnton, but not a single Daresbury man attained double figures. -- Warrington Municipal Officers' Guild continue to do well and on Saturday they accounted for Wilderspool Brewery by 61. For the winners D. Holland bowled splendidly taking six wiekets foe eight runs. He also did the " hat trick." R. Price (25) and A. T. Hallaway (17) batted well for their respective scores. Sankey Wire Mills journeyed to Lymm, but the home team proved too good for them and won by 16. S. Pollitt was in grand form for the winners and carried out his bat with 49 to his credit. W. Woodcock made the best effort for the Wire Mills, his innings realizing 18. 'Bowling. Lancashire bowlers gave a good account of themselves against Cheshire and Yorkshire, and won by 69 points. Several Warrington players did service for their county. G. Ball, jun., beat G. b'. Dickenson, Halifax, by 21-18, whilst A. Gleave had an easy task in disposing of H. Jones, Low Moor, and won by 21-5. T. Ellison, who won the Individual Merit Competition, wont down to J. West, of Taylor Hill, by 21-14. For the special gold medal for the Crosfteld Cup, H. S. Connolly, of the Victoria green, hes the hest record, for he won against Staffordshire 21-5, and he beat F. Eastwood, of Brighouse by 21-8. The return encounter, which will finally decide the event, will take place in Yorkshire on July 25. The works competition continues to create groat interest. On Seturday there was a first round enconnter between Thewlie and Griffiths and Whitecross No. 2, the wire workers being successful by 31 points. The closest game was 'between G. Ball, sen. captain of Thewlis and Griflithe;and W. Bali. ,The dayers were repeatedly level and at the nineteenth end the situation nes 12-12. Then G.Ball got two aed led 14 —42,but W. Ball at once followed with a couple and gaining a single immediately afterwards won by 15-14. In the eecond round Houghton's No. 1, settled Fletcher's No. 1 aspirations by 22 points. There was a capital encounter between E. Bailey and W.Gleave. The contestants were equal at 4 and then Gleave forged ahead. At the eighteenth end, however, Bailey caught him up and the score was 10-10. Then Gleave got in a' couple, but Bailey was alert and had the run of successes, and although Gleave fought well he had te admit defeat by 15-14. The other match was between Crosfleld's No. 2, and Wire Ropery No. 1, Crosfield's being victorious by 33 points. The closest game was between D. Stokes and W. Appleton. Stokes carried all before him at first and led 12-3. Appleton, however, got into stride and gradually piling on points, drew level at 13-13. He then capped his achievements by getting a couple which gave him the victory by 15-13. The following is the draw for the third round 1— Whitecross No. 1 v. Crosfleld's No. 2 ; Whitecross No. 2or Castle Rubber v. Rylands No. 1; L. tzt N.-W. or Crosfleld's No. 1 v. Monks Hall„No. 1 ; Houghton's No. 1 v. P. 8c K. -- There will be no matches played until July 18th, as two annual mains are being played on the green. The contest for the Sir Gilbert Greenall Shield presented to the Independent Order of Ochifellows was decided at Sankey on Saturday. The final brought together Bro. H. Ashbrook, " Perseverance" Lodge, and Bro. T. Litton, " Friendship" Lodge, P.G.M., some fine play resulting in Bro. Ashbrook carrying off the shield. The competition throughput was a great success. •Cycling. The attendances at the club functions last Saturday appeared about equally divided, somewhere in the region' of a dozen members carrying out the programme to Acton Bridge, whilst a similar number had departed over night to pay a visit to the Exhibition, London i being reached n the early hours of the morning. A very interesting time was spent by the members during their all-too-brief stay, in viewing the many and varied attractions, the majority arriving home again on Tuesday morning. A small contingent were out at Warburton on Tuesday evening, the puncture fiend being much in evidence during the return journey. -- Wednesday evening found almost thirty members at Sankey where a few games were played off in the handicap, which is now nearing completion. -- To-day the annual visit- to Farndon takes place, a goodly number generally contriving to put in a week- end at this lovely spot on the banks of the Dee.

TANNERS' LABOURER'S SHOCKING DEATH. Fatal Fall Into a Tan Pit. A shocking fatality occurred at the tannery of Messrs. Randall Bros., Ltd., Tanners-lane, on Thurs- day morning. Henry McMahon (3:3), tanners' labourer, 15' Hardy-street, was following his employ- ment there along with another labourer, Patrick Ryan. They were removing hides from one tan pit to another and deceased was wheeling a barrow over a plank, when the barrow overbalanced and lie was throwu into a pit of liquor, the barrow and the contents falling with him. Ryan raised an alarm, and he was got out in a very exhausted condition. Dr. Adams was sent for and ordered his removal home, where ha was again seen by the doctor, but died at 12 o'clock.
